CAC, LTV and Payback

Can we afford to acquire this customer, and how long until they have paid us back for the privilege of having them?

A reading on the arithmetic every product manager eventually has to defend in a room full of people holding a spreadsheet.

A number on a slide, a question in the room

On the second Tuesday of March 2026, Ananya Rao stood in front of eight people in a glass-walled conference room on the fourth floor of a WeWork in Bengaluru's Koramangala, advancing to slide fourteen of a growth deck she had rebuilt three times that week. Ananya was Head of Growth Product at Bhavya Fitness, a two-and-a-half-year-old subscription app offering live and on-demand workout classes, priced at ₹799 a month, competing for the attention of the same urban, gym-curious twenty-five-to-forty-year-olds that half a dozen well-funded rivals were also chasing. The company had just closed a Series B, and the question on the table was not abstract: should Bhavya commit an incremental ₹40 lakh a month to performance marketing, timed to a sponsorship slot during the Indian Premier League cricket season, when eyeballs would be cheap to reach but expensive to convert?

The Chief Financial Officer, a former investment banker named Kabir Sethi, was not interested in reach or impressions. He wanted to know what Ananya called, without flinching, the blended customer acquisition cost, and what it implied for how fast that ₹40 lakh would come back to the company as cash. "If we're going to burn our runway faster," he said, tapping his pen against the table, "I want to know in months, not vibes, when we get it back." Bhavya's monthly marketing spend was already ₹85 lakh, bringing in roughly 5,100 new paying subscribers a month; churn had crept up over the last two quarters from 5 percent to 6 percent monthly, which nobody in the room had yet connected to the CFO's question, but which was about to become the crux of it. If Ananya got the underlying arithmetic wrong — if she reported a payback period that looked shorter than it truly was, or leaned on a lifetime value number that assumed customers stuck around longer than they actually did — Bhavya could commit real capital against an acquisition channel that would never earn its keep, and find out only two quarters later, once the runway had visibly shortened and the board had lost patience. Getting it right, conversely, would let her make the case for exactly the right amount of aggression: neither timid capital allocation that ceded the IPL season to a rival, nor a reckless bet dressed up as growth.

The idea, defined plainly

Customer acquisition cost (CAC) is what a company spends, on average, to acquire one paying customer over a given period — total spend on sales and marketing divided by the number of new customers that spend produced. Lifetime value (LTV) is the total gross profit a company can expect to earn from a customer over the entire span of their relationship with the company, not their revenue, but what is left after the direct cost of serving them. Payback period is the number of months it takes for the gross profit generated by a customer to equal what it cost to acquire them — the point at which that customer stops being a liability on the cash flow statement and starts being a source of it. Together, the three numbers answer a single underlying question: can this company afford to keep acquiring customers the way it currently does, and for how long must it wait, and how much capital must it be willing to have tied up, before each new customer pays the company back for having acquired them at all.

Nobody signed a single paper inventing these terms the way Frederick Taylor is credited with scientific management or Peter Drucker with management by objectives. The vocabulary of CAC, LTV and payback crystallised gradually inside venture capital and inside the subscription-software industry through the 2000s, as companies stopped selling one-time licenses and started selling recurring access — a shift that made the old question, "did this sale make money," insufficient, because a single month's revenue from a subscriber rarely covered what it cost to win them. It needed to be replaced with a question about the whole relationship. The Boston-based venture capitalist David Skok, writing on his blog For Entrepreneurs from around 2008 onward, did more than almost anyone to popularise the specific ratios — most durably the rule of thumb that a healthy subscription business keeps its lifetime value at three times or more its acquisition cost, and recovers that acquisition cost within about twelve months. Growth-stage investors such as Bessemer Venture Partners later folded the same logic into the standard metrics memo that accompanies almost every SaaS fundraising process today. The sentence Ananya could say in that room without sounding glib was this: unit economics only become durable when the profit a customer generates, discounted for how long that customer actually stays, comfortably exceeds — and quickly recovers — what it cost to bring them in the door.

Figure 1. CAC is a cost of entry; LTV is what the relationship is worth once it exists; payback is the bridge between the two, measured in time rather than money.

How it actually works, step by step

The mechanics look simple on a slide and hide several judgment calls in practice, which is exactly where most of the disagreement in that Bengaluru conference room would eventually surface. The first step is to define the period and the spend that counts as acquisition cost: not just the media budget handed to Meta and Google, but the salaries of the growth and performance-marketing team, the cost of the creative agency, the tools used to run campaigns, and, in a business with any outbound sales motion, the commissions and base pay of the people closing deals. Bhavya's ₹85 lakh figure that month was, refreshingly, already fully loaded in this sense — Ananya had insisted on that discipline a year earlier after discovering that an earlier "CAC" figure had quietly excluded her own team's salaries, making the number look better than the cash reality.

The second step is to decide what counts as a "new customer" for the denominator — usually a paying subscriber who converts within an attribution window, not a free trial signup, not an app download, and not a lead who later churns before ever paying. Divide the fully loaded spend by that count and CAC falls out. The third step, and the one that separates a useful number from a decorative one, is to build gross profit per customer per month: subscription revenue minus the direct cost of delivering the service — for Bhavya, the cost of streaming infrastructure, trainer payouts for live classes, and payment-gateway fees — expressed as a margin, not as revenue on its own. The fourth step is to translate observed monthly churn into an expected customer lifetime, using the simple relationship that average lifetime in months is approximately one divided by the monthly churn rate, which is the step most practitioners perform silently in a spreadsheet cell without ever saying out loud that they are assuming the future will look like the recent past. Multiply gross profit per month by that expected lifetime and LTV appears. Divide CAC by gross profit per month, not by LTV, and payback period appears — a distinction worth pausing on, because payback is a statement about cash flow timing, and time-in-months has nothing to do with how long the customer eventually stays after that point; a customer could pay back the company in three months and then churn in month four, or stay for three years, and the payback number alone will not tell you which.

The arithmetic, walked through in full

Ananya's base case, built from March 2026 actuals, looked like this. Monthly fully loaded acquisition spend of ₹85,00,000 produced 5,100 new paying subscribers, for a blended CAC of ₹85,00,000 ÷ 5,100 ≈ ₹1,667 per customer. The average subscription price was ₹799 a month, and Bhavya's direct cost of service — streaming, trainer payouts, payment processing — ran at 30 percent of revenue, leaving a gross margin of 70 percent, or ₹559 of gross profit per customer per month. Monthly churn, measured over the trailing quarter, sat at 6 percent, implying an expected average customer lifetime of 1 ÷ 0.06 ≈ 16.7 months. Lifetime value, then, was ₹559 × 16.7 ≈ ₹9,335 per customer — against a CAC of ₹1,667, an LTV-to-CAC ratio of roughly 5.6 to 1, comfortably clearing the conventional 3-to-1 bar. Payback period was CAC divided by monthly gross profit: ₹1,667 ÷ ₹559 ≈ 3.0 months. On paper, an enviable set of numbers: a healthy ratio and a fast payback, the combination that lets a company reinvest aggressively.

The second pass is where the number stopped being reassuring and started being useful, because Ananya changed one input at a time rather than all at once. First, she asked what happened to the picture if churn — which had already drifted from 5 to 6 percent over two quarters — continued to 9 percent, a plausible outcome if the IPL-season push pulled in a less-committed, deal-seeking cohort rather than genuinely motivated fitness customers. At 9 percent monthly churn, expected lifetime falls to 1 ÷ 0.09 ≈ 11.1 months, and LTV falls with it, to ₹559 × 11.1 ≈ ₹6,205 — an LTV-to-CAC ratio of 3.7 to 1, thinner but still above the conventional floor. What did not move at all was the payback period: it remained ₹1,667 ÷ ₹559 ≈ 3.0 months, because payback depends only on CAC and monthly gross profit, not on how long the customer eventually stays. That asymmetry is precisely the kind of distinction that separates someone who has internalised the mechanics from someone reciting the vocabulary — a company can have a fast, reassuring payback period and still be building a business whose long-run value is quietly eroding, because payback and lifetime value are answering different questions and can move independently of one another.

Second, Ananya modelled what a genuinely incremental IPL push would cost, rather than assuming the new spend would convert at the existing blended CAC. Cricket-season inventory on Meta and Google gets more expensive as every consumer brand in the country bids for the same eyeballs; her media buyer's estimate was that the marginal cost per acquired subscriber on that specific push would run closer to ₹2,400, not ₹1,667. At that marginal CAC, holding the base-case 6 percent churn, payback stretches to ₹2,400 ÷ ₹559 ≈ 4.3 months, and LTV-to-CAC falls to ₹9,335 ÷ ₹2,400 ≈ 3.9 to 1 — still defensible, but a materially different bet than the blended 3-month, 5.6-to-1 picture on the same slide fourteen that had started the conversation.

Eight distinctions a learner must own

1. Blended CAC is a description of the past; marginal CAC is the decision that matters

Blended CAC averages every channel and every customer together into one comforting number. But the decision in front of Ananya was never "should we keep doing what we're doing" — it was "should we spend the next ₹40 lakh," and the next rupee of spend does not buy customers at the average cost, it buys them at whatever the next-cheapest available customer costs on the margin, which is very often higher than the blended average because the cheapest channels — organic search, referral, word of mouth — are usually saturated first. Anyone who defends a budget increase by quoting blended CAC is answering a question nobody asked.

2. LTV is a forecast wearing the clothes of a fact

The moment a churn rate is used to imply an "expected lifetime," the calculation has silently assumed that the future will resemble the recent past — that a customer acquired this month will churn at the same rate, month after month, as customers acquired a year ago. Cohorts change: a rushed IPL-season sign-up is a different customer, with a different reason for joining, than someone who found Bhavya through a friend's recommendation in a quiet month. Treating LTV as observed rather than assumed is the single most common way this metric misleads.

3. Payback is a statement about cash, not about profitability

A three-month payback period tells a CFO how long the company's cash is tied up in a given customer before that customer becomes a net contributor to gross profit. It says nothing about whether Bhavya as a whole is profitable — fixed costs, engineering salaries, office rent and every other line below gross margin are entirely absent from the calculation. A company can report an excellent payback period on every individual customer and still lose money overall, because payback is unit-level and the P&L is company-level.

4. Revenue is not gross profit, and using revenue inflates every downstream number

It is common, and tempting, to compute LTV against subscription price rather than against the margin left after the direct cost of serving the customer. Doing so overstates LTV by whatever fraction the cost of goods sold represents — for Bhavya, using revenue instead of the 70-percent-margin gross profit figure would have overstated LTV by nearly a third, turning a defensible 5.6-to-1 ratio into a misleadingly flattering 8-to-1.

5. A simple LTV ignores the time value of money

Nine thousand rupees of profit collected steadily over sixteen months is worth less today than nine thousand rupees collected up front, because capital has a cost and money in the future is less certain than money now. Rigorous treatments discount each future month's expected gross profit back to the present before summing them into LTV; the simple version most operating teams use, including Ananya's base case above, is an approximation that overstates true economic value, more so the longer the expected customer lifetime runs.

6. What counts as "acquisition cost" is a policy choice, not a natural fact

Whether to include the growth team's salaries, the design agency's retainer, or a sponsorship's brand-building spillover in CAC is a judgment call, and different teams within the same company routinely make it differently, which is why comparing CAC figures across companies — or even across quarters inside one company — requires first confirming that the definition has not quietly shifted underneath the number.

7. Aggregate figures hide cohort-level decay

A single blended LTV-to-CAC ratio for "this quarter" can look perfectly healthy while the trend underneath it is deteriorating — CAC rising channel by channel as auctions get more competitive, retention softening as the top of the funnel widens to less-qualified prospects — because the aggregate number is a lagging average of a mix that has been quietly getting worse. Only a cohort-by-cohort view, tracking each acquisition month's customers against their own eventual retention curve, will surface that decay before it becomes an emergency.

8. None of these three numbers explains why a customer stays or leaves

CAC, LTV and payback are accounting constructs built from a churn rate and a margin; they describe the financial consequence of retention, not its cause. They cannot tell Ananya whether subscribers are staying because the live classes are genuinely good, because a rival's app crashed, or because cancellation is inconveniently buried in a settings menu — and mistaking a favourable ratio for evidence of product quality, rather than treating it as a number that still needs a "why" behind it, is a quiet trap for teams that stop asking qualitative questions once the unit economics look acceptable.

Consumer, B2B and marketplace — and early-stage versus scale

The shape of this arithmetic changes with the kind of business wrapped around it, and Bhavya's case sits at only one point on a wide spectrum. Consider a second, fictional company: Bhairavi Cloud, a Hyderabad-based B2B software vendor selling procurement software to hospital chains, with an average contract value of ₹18 lakh a year and a sales cycle that runs six to nine months, involving a regional sales manager, a solutions engineer, and often a trip to meet the hospital's finance committee in person. Bhairavi's CAC is an order of magnitude higher than Bhavya's in absolute rupees, driven almost entirely by fully loaded sales compensation and travel rather than digital media, and its payback period, sixteen months by the time it was last measured, would look alarming by Bhavya's consumer standard. But a sixteen-month payback is entirely normal, even good, in enterprise software, because Bhairavi's customers rarely churn inside of three years once their procurement workflows are embedded, and because existing customers routinely buy more modules over time — a phenomenon called net revenue retention that consumer subscription businesses like Bhavya's rarely enjoy at the same scale, since a fitness subscriber has no adjacent product to expand into. The same three numbers, applied faithfully, point B2B companies toward tolerating slower payback in exchange for a much larger and more durable eventual LTV.

A third shape appears in a marketplace business, illustrated by another fictional company, Bhilwara Haat, which connects small textile mills around Bhilwara, Rajasthan, to retail buyers across India. Marketplaces have two customers, not one — the mills supplying inventory and the retailers buying it — and CAC, LTV and payback need to be computed separately for each side, because the economics rarely match: a buyer might be cheap to acquire and highly valuable, while a quality supplier might be expensive to onboard and moderately valuable on their own, yet essential to the platform because their inventory is what makes buyer acquisition possible in the first place. The common mistake at a company like Bhilwara Haat is to compute one blended marketplace-wide CAC and LTV, which obscures the reality that the two sides subsidise each other — spending to acquire suppliers can be justified by the buyer value it unlocks, a form of cross-side value that a single-sided consumer or B2B business like Bhavya or Bhairavi never has to reason about. Finally, the same numbers behave differently at different stages of a company's life: an early-stage company, with only a handful of months of retention data, is often computing LTV from a churn curve that has not yet had time to fully play out, which tends to make lifetime value look better than it eventually proves to be, while a large, mature company has enough history to compute true cohort-level payback curves and marginal CAC by channel, but usually faces the opposite problem — a market approaching saturation, where CAC creeps upward every quarter regardless of how disciplined the marketing team is.

Figure 2. Both curves cross the ₹1,667 CAC line at roughly the same point — near month three — because payback depends only on CAC and monthly gross profit. The curves diverge afterward: the weaker cohort flattens well below the base case, meaning payback speed alone would not have warned the board that churn was quietly worsening lifetime value.

Where teams get this wrong

The first common mistake shows up as a board slide reporting an LTV-to-CAC ratio north of eight or ten, while the company's cash position keeps tightening despite that apparently glowing number. The underlying error is almost always that LTV was computed on revenue rather than gross profit, or that the assumed customer lifetime was extrapolated indefinitely from an early, thin retention curve rather than grounded in a full cohort's observed behaviour. The cheapest diagnostic is to recompute the ratio using only actual gross margin dollars and only the retention data the company has actually observed to date, refusing to extrapolate a churn curve out past the number of months of real cohort history available.

The second mistake shows up as a reported payback period of two or three months that keeps not translating into the cash relief the finance team expected. Underneath it, the spend decision is usually being made against a blended CAC that is pulled down by cheap organic and referral customers, while the actual incremental dollars are being poured into a paid channel whose true marginal CAC runs two or three times higher. The fix is to segment CAC by channel and to fund each channel's spend against its own payback, never against the company-wide blend.

The third mistake shows up as a board that keeps approving ever-larger marketing budgets on the strength of a single quarter's ratio, unaware that the trend beneath it has been quietly worsening for two quarters running — CAC creeping up channel by channel, retention softening as the funnel widens. The remedy is cheap and almost entirely a matter of discipline: plot LTV-to-CAC and payback period by acquisition cohort over time, not as a single current snapshot, and insist that any budget conversation include the trend line, not just this month's point estimate.

The fourth mistake, common at companies with any enterprise sales motion, shows up as a sales team celebrating a large new account whose acquisition cost was extraordinary, waved through as "strategic" without any further scrutiny. The underlying problem is that "strategic" is being used as a substitute for arithmetic rather than a category with its own arithmetic — the honest fix is to model that account's expansion-adjusted lifetime value explicitly, including any anticipated growth in the relationship, and to require that even a strategic account clear a payback horizon the company has deliberately chosen to tolerate, rather than one nobody ever specified.

What good looks like

Before the Tuesday board meeting, Ananya had rebuilt her deck around exactly this discipline. She broke the blended ₹1,667 CAC apart by channel and found that referral-driven subscribers, who signed up because an existing member had invited them, carried a marginal CAC near ₹310 — mostly the cost of the referral credit itself — and churned at 4 percent a month rather than 6, a materially better cohort by every measure that mattered. Google Search, by contrast, ran a marginal CAC of about ₹1,900 but still cleared a defensible payback under four months. The prospective IPL sponsorship push, whose true marginal cost nobody at the table could yet pin down with confidence, she proposed treating as a bounded pilot: a capped ten-day spend with an explicit stop-loss if the observed marginal CAC crossed ₹3,000, rather than the full ₹40 lakh committed up front on the strength of a blended number that had never been tested against that specific channel. She recommended the board approve doubling the referral incentive budget immediately, since its economics were already proven, expanding Search spend within its known payback window, and running the IPL sponsorship as a measured experiment rather than a bet — three decisions, each backed by its own marginal arithmetic, in place of one undifferentiated request to "increase the growth budget."

The decision, and what to carry forward

Kabir Sethi approved the staged plan that Tuesday, with the stop-loss written into the board minutes rather than left as a verbal understanding, and asked for the channel-level payback curves to appear on every future board deck rather than a single blended ratio. Ananya's reasoning, restated plainly, was that the question "can we afford to acquire this customer" only has a stable answer once acquisition cost, gross profit, and expected retention are each defined precisely and applied consistently — and that a single attractive-looking ratio, however impressive on a slide, is never a substitute for knowing which specific channel, at which specific marginal cost, is actually generating the number being celebrated. The natural next things for a reader to study are how these unit economics roll up into the recurring-revenue metrics — ARR, MRR, churn and net revenue retention — that investors track quarter over quarter; how to model LTV directly from an empirical retention curve rather than a single average churn rate; how the economics differ again across acquisition channels themselves, from paid search to influencer partnerships to enterprise sales; how these figures change shape as they are tracked at each stage of a marketing and sales funnel rather than only at the moment of conversion; how a full cohort-level profit-and-loss statement extends payback thinking into a genuine forecasting tool; and how blended and marginal economics interact at a company's actual scale, where the two numbers can tell very different stories from the same underlying business.

Two questions worth sitting with. First: if your own team reported a payback period of three months this quarter, would you know, without asking anyone else, whether that number was computed on blended or marginal CAC — and would the answer change what you did next?

Second: when a healthy LTV-to-CAC ratio and a worsening retention trend are both true of the same business at the same time, which one would your organisation notice first, and which one would it act on?

CAC, LTV and Payback

Three numbers that look like measurements and are in fact conventions — and the judgement required to know which convention is load-bearing in the decision actually in front of you.

A reading for the practitioner who already computes these numbers correctly and now has to referee a disagreement between two people who both computed them correctly and arrived at opposite recommendations.

Section oneTwo rooms, one arithmetic

On the morning of 11 February 2026, in a converted textile-mill office off Pune's Senapati Bapat Road, Meera Iyengar was looking at a slide she had refused to present the previous week. Meera was Vice-President of Product at Pushkar Devices, a seven-year-old company that made a bench-top point-of-care blood analyser and sold it, bundled with a subscription software layer and a monthly consumables contract, to independent diagnostic laboratories and single-doctor clinics across tier-two and tier-three India. Pushkar had 2,180 machines installed, was adding about 180 a quarter through a field sales force of forty-one people, and had eleven months of runway. The slide said the company's customer acquisition cost was ₹1,16,667. Meera's objection was that the number was true and useless. It counted the fully loaded cost of the sales organisation divided by installations, and it entirely omitted the fact that Pushkar sold each ₹1,42,000 device to the laboratory for ₹45,000 in order to get it onto the bench at all. The ₹97,000 difference was booked in cost of goods sold, where it dutifully depressed gross margin and was never mentioned in the same sentence as the word "acquisition."

The decision on the table was whether to raise the device price to ₹1,10,000 and cut the subsidy. The Chief Financial Officer, Sandeep Bhatia, had modelled it and found payback falling from roughly fourteen months to under eleven. The Vice-President of Sales, Harish Nadkarni, had run a limited pilot in Nashik and Kolhapur and reported that at ₹1,10,000 the sales cycle lengthened from six weeks to fourteen and installation volume fell by close to half. Both men were competent, both had used the same three metrics, and they disagreed completely. Meera's job that quarter was not to compute anything. It was to work out which of them was reasoning about the right quantity.

Eleven hundred kilometres away, in a Gurugram office on the same morning, Rohan Malaviya was facing a structurally identical problem wearing entirely different clothes. Rohan was Head of Product at Pratyush AI, a four-year-old company selling an AI system that read incoming vendor contracts for large Indian manufacturers, extracted obligations, and flagged deviations from a company's own playbook. Pratyush had fifty-eight enterprise customers, an average contract value of ₹9.6 lakh a year, and a sales motion that consumed ₹4.75 crore of fully loaded sales and marketing in the preceding half-year. That arithmetic produced a customer acquisition cost of ₹9.5 lakh — slightly under one year of contract value, which the board considered excellent. The difficulty was the other side of the ratio. Pratyush's gross margin was 62 per cent, not the 80 per cent the board's SaaS comparables assumed, because every contract processed consumed model inference. Its customers expanded usage at about 0.9 per cent a month. Its logo churn was 1.2 per cent a month. And depending on which of six entirely defensible conventions Rohan applied, lifetime value came out anywhere between ₹13.9 lakh and ₹66.7 lakh — a range wide enough to make the same company look like a 1.5-to-1 disaster or a 7-to-1 compounding machine.

The argument of this reading is that CAC, LTV and payback are not three measurements of a business. They are three modelling choices about a business, and the discipline that separates an expert from a competent practitioner is knowing exactly which choice each number is smuggling, and which of those choices the decision in front of you is actually sensitive to.

Section twoThe idea, its history, and the schools that disagree about it

The definitions can be stated tightly. Customer acquisition cost is the fully loaded cost of sales and marketing attributable to winning one incremental customer. Lifetime value is the present value of the contribution margin a customer is expected to generate over the remainder of the relationship. Payback period is the number of periods until the cumulative contribution margin from an acquired cohort equals the cost of acquiring it. Each definition contains a word doing enormous quiet work: attributable, expected, present value, cohort. Practitioners who fight about these metrics are almost never fighting about arithmetic; they are fighting about those four words.

The intellectual history runs in two streams that met late and have never fully merged. The first is direct and database marketing. Catalogue retailers in the United States and the United Kingdom through the 1970s and 1980s had a genuinely hard problem — a mailing was expensive, a buyer might respond once or fifteen times — and they solved it with recency-frequency-monetary scoring and with the first formal customer lifetime value calculations. Frederick Reichheld and W. Earl Sasser's 1990 Harvard Business Review article "Zero Defections: Quality Comes to Services" moved the idea from the mailroom to the boardroom by arguing that retention, not acquisition, was where the profit lived. Robert Blattberg and John Deighton's 1996 HBR piece "Manage Marketing by the Customer Equity Test" made the balance-sheet argument explicit: a firm is, in one reading, the sum of the discounted margins of its customers. Sunil Gupta, Donald Lehmann and Jennifer Stuart's 2004 work valuing customers connected customer equity to observable firm value, and Peter Fader and Bruce Hardie at Wharton built the probabilistic machinery — the Pareto/NBD and beta-geometric families — that models customers as a heterogeneous population of individually simple behaviours rather than as one average customer.

The second stream is venture capital and subscription software, and it is far more recent and far more influential in the rooms most product managers sit in. When software moved from perpetual licences to recurring subscriptions in the 2000s, a single period's revenue stopped covering the cost of the sale, and investors needed a fast way to sort businesses whose income statements all looked terrible. David Skok's writing from about 2008 popularised the two heuristics that have since become almost liturgical: keep lifetime value above three times acquisition cost, and recover acquisition cost inside twelve months. Bessemer Venture Partners folded the same logic into the metrics memo that accompanies most growth-stage fundraising. Andreessen Horowitz's widely circulated essay on startup metrics added the warnings. Bill Gurley's 2012 essay "The Dangerous Seduction of the Lifetime Value (LTV) Formula" is the canonical dissent, and after the 2022 capital-market repricing — when growth stopped being free and CAC payback replaced growth rate as the headline number in most board decks — its argument won a great deal of ground.

Four schools now disagree in ways that matter, and the useful discipline is to state precisely which proposition each would and would not sign.

The ratio school holds that LTV-to-CAC above three, with payback inside a year, is the right sorting device. It would sign: at portfolio scale, across many companies, this pair of numbers separates durable businesses from doomed ones better than any other cheap test. It would not sign: that three is an optimum rather than a floor, or that the ratio should govern any individual channel or quarter decision. A business running at eight-to-one is not eight-to-one healthy; it is almost certainly underspending on acquisition and leaving growth on the table, which is a failure of ambition dressed as prudence.

The cash school, which has been ascendant since 2022, holds that lifetime value is unknowable and therefore inadmissible. It would sign: the only numbers a board should act on are payback measured in realised cash and the burn multiple — net burn divided by net new ARR — because both rest on money that has actually moved. It would not sign: that LTV belongs in a board deck at all, on the grounds that a forecast placed next to a measurement gets treated as a measurement. Its strongest evidence is the graveyard of 2021-vintage companies whose LTV-to-CAC slides were immaculate right up until the cash ran out.

The probabilistic school holds that the standard practitioner formula is not an approximation but a mis-specification. It would sign: customers differ in their propensity to leave, that heterogeneity is the dominant feature of every retention curve ever observed, and dividing one by an average churn rate produces an answer that is biased, usually downward, often by a factor of two. It would not sign: that a single churn number can stand in for a retention curve, ever. Its evidence is that observed cohort hazard rates decline over time in essentially every subscription business, which a constant-churn model cannot produce.

The incrementality school comes from marketing econometrics rather than finance and attacks the denominator. It would sign: a customer who would have arrived anyway is not an acquired customer, so the only defensible CAC is one whose denominator comes from a holdout or geographic experiment. It would not sign: that platform-reported conversions can be used as the denominator for any decision involving incremental spend. Its evidence is the long series of large-advertiser holdout tests in which switching off brand-keyword search or retargeting moved attributed conversions enormously and total conversions barely at all.

There is a fifth position worth naming because it appears whenever a strategy team enters the room: the option school, which treats acquisition spend as the purchase of an asset with option value — an installed base, a data advantage, a bench slot a competitor now cannot occupy. It would sign: that a short payback target, rigorously enforced, can be actively value-destroying in a market with winner-take-most dynamics. It would not sign: that this licenses unbounded spend, though in practice it is the argument most often abused to license exactly that.

Section threeMechanics: the four places the arithmetic bends

An expert's version of this calculation differs from a competent one in four specific places. Each is a step usually performed silently inside a spreadsheet cell.

3.1 The retention curve is not exponential, and the reason matters

The formula that expected lifetime equals one divided by the monthly churn rate is exactly right for a population in which every customer has the same constant monthly probability of leaving. No such population has ever been observed. Real cohorts are mixtures. Consider a cohort of 1,000 customers that is in truth 600 "tourists" with a 20 per cent monthly probability of leaving and 400 "residents" with a 3 per cent probability. Nobody at the company knows the mixture exists; all they see is the aggregate.

In the first month, 120 tourists and 12 residents leave, so observed churn is 13.2 per cent, implying an expected lifetime of 7.6 months. The truth is that expected lifetime is 0.6 × (1/0.20) + 0.4 × (1/0.03) = 3.0 + 13.3 = 16.3 months, more than twice the naive figure. Worse, the naive figure is not stably wrong. By month twelve the tourists have almost all gone; the surviving population is 87 per cent residents, and observed monthly churn has fallen to 5.6 per cent, implying a lifetime of 17.9 months. Nobody's behaviour changed. Only the mix did.

3.2 Payback has an asymptote, and naive payback does not know about it

The second bend is that dividing CAC by monthly contribution margin ignores the fact that some of the cohort leaves before payback arrives. Cumulative contribution per acquired customer after n months, with monthly contribution m and monthly retention r, is:

Cum(n) = m × (1 − rn) ÷ (1 − r)   →   ceiling of m ÷ (1 − r) as n grows

Take m = ₹4,000 and r = 0.94, that is 6 per cent monthly churn. The ceiling is ₹4,000 ÷ 0.06 = ₹66,667. A CAC of ₹12,000 gives a naive payback of 3.0 months and a true payback of 3.2 — the correction is trivial. A CAC of ₹35,000 gives a naive payback of 8.75 months and a true payback of 12.0 — the correction is 37 per cent and changes which side of the twelve-month line the business sits on. And a CAC of ₹70,000 gives a naive payback of 17.5 months and a true payback that does not exist: the cohort mathematically cannot repay it, because ₹70,000 is above the ceiling. Naive arithmetic returns a confident finite answer for a cohort that will never break even. This is not a rare pathology. It is the standard shape of a consumer subscription business in its second year of paid-channel expansion.

Figure 2. Cumulative contribution per acquired customer flattens toward a hard ceiling set by monthly margin divided by churn. Below the ceiling, naive payback understates the true figure by a margin that widens with churn and with CAC. Above the ceiling, naive payback is not merely inaccurate; it is answering a question with no answer. The diagnostic an expert runs before any payback discussion is a single division: is CAC below m ÷ (1 − r)?

3.3 Discounting, expansion, and the divergence nobody notices

The third bend is the present-value step. For constant retention r, monthly contribution m and monthly discount rate d, the standard closed form is the margin multiple:

LTV = m × r ÷ (1 + d − r)

Introduce expansion at monthly rate g and the retention term becomes r(1+g). This is where the expert's alarm should sound, because the series only converges if r(1+g) < 1 + d. In a healthy enterprise business with net revenue retention above 100 per cent, r(1+g) exceeds one, and the only thing preventing lifetime value from being infinite is the discount rate — a parameter that, in most operating companies, nobody has ever formally chosen. The number on the slide is therefore almost entirely a function of an unexamined assumption. Rohan's Pratyush AI numbers make this concrete.

3.4 The denominator: attribution is not incrementality, and lag is not neutral

The fourth bend is the one most often invisible to product managers because it lives in the marketing organisation. Two distortions compound. The first is attribution: a platform reports the conversions it can claim, not the conversions it caused. In a geographic holdout run across twelve matched Indian cities — six treated, six dark — treated cities produced 1,000 new customers and control cities 640, implying 360 incremental customers, while the advertising platforms claimed 820. Computed honestly, the marginal CAC on that spend is 2.3 times the reported figure. Brand-keyword search and retargeting are the two channels where this gap is routinely largest, and they are also, not coincidentally, the two channels that always look cheapest on a blended dashboard.

The second distortion is lag. If acquisition spend is growing 10 per cent a month and customers convert with a four-month lag, then dividing this month's spend by this month's new customers compares a rupee figure that is 1.104 = 1.46 times larger than the spend that actually bought those customers. CAC is overstated by 46 per cent. Reverse the sign and the consequence is far more dangerous: a company that cuts marketing spend 15 per cent a month while conversions from earlier, larger spend keep arriving will report a CAC that improves spectacularly for exactly as long as the pipeline takes to drain. Expert practitioners cohort-match spend to conversions by acquisition date rather than by calendar month, and treat any sudden CAC improvement that coincides with a budget cut as an artefact until proven otherwise.

Section fourWhen the framework applies, and when it actively misleads

The framework rests on four conditions, each of which can be stated as a testable claim and checked against a specific business.

Condition one: acquisition cost is separable from cost to serve. The test is whether you can point to a rupee and say unambiguously which bucket it belongs in. For Pratyush AI this passes cleanly — a sales engineer's salary is acquisition, an inference token is service. For Pushkar Devices it fails outright. The ₹97,000 device subsidy is booked as cost of goods sold and is economically indistinguishable from a sales incentive. Meera's insistence on recomputing CAC as ₹1,16,667 + ₹97,000 = ₹2,13,667 is not a bookkeeping preference; it is the difference between a fourteen-month payback and a twenty-four-month one on the figures Sandeep Bhatia had been presenting.

Condition two: the customer is the right unit. The test is whether revenue and retention are properties of an individual account. Pratyush AI passes. Pushkar Devices does not, quite: the paying unit is a laboratory, but the economically meaningful unit is the bench slot, since a lab with two analysers from different vendors will consolidate within a year. A two-sided marketplace fails this condition entirely, because value is created at the intersection of two customer populations.

Condition three: past retention predicts future retention. The test is whether cohorts acquired twelve months apart, at the same tenure, retain similarly. For Pushkar this holds well; diagnostic labs behave the same way in 2023 and 2026. For Pratyush AI it may not hold at all, because the product category is four years old, the competitive set changes quarterly, and the price a customer will accept in 2028 depends on where model costs have gone.

Condition four: the margin structure is stable. The test is whether a customer acquired today will be served at roughly today's unit cost. Pushkar passes; consumables costs move with commodity prices, slowly. Pratyush AI fails in both directions simultaneously: inference cost per contract has fallen about 40 per cent a year, which pushes margin up, while competitive pressure on price pushes it down, and the two are not independent because the same cost decline is what enables competitors to undercut.

The framework is actively misleading — not merely imprecise — in three situations. The first is a business whose retention depends on a network that is still forming, where early cohorts are systematically worse than later ones and any LTV anchored on observed history understates the asset being built. The second is a business in the middle of a pricing or packaging change, where the mixture of old and new cohorts makes every aggregate number a chimera. The third, and the most common, is any business where the decision under discussion is a step change in spend rather than a marginal one: hiring twelve enterprise sellers is not "more CAC," it is a new cost structure with a six-month productivity ramp during which reported CAC will be catastrophic and the correct decision may nonetheless be to proceed.

Section fiveHard edges, and the seams between departments

Multi-product. When a customer buys two products, whose CAC was it? The three conventions in use are first-product attribution (clean, understates the second product's economics), proportional allocation by revenue (defensible, arbitrary), and land-and-expand accounting in which acquisition cost sits entirely with the entry product and everything after is treated as expansion with near-zero acquisition cost. The third is the most common and produces the reliable pathology of a second product that looks wildly profitable and a first product that looks unfundable, leading companies to underinvest in exactly the wedge that made the second product reachable.

Two-sided. Supply-side and demand-side economics must be computed separately and then connected, and the connection is where most of the error lives. Crediting a supplier's acquisition with the buyer retention it enables is correct; also reporting improved buyer LTV at the better retention rate double-counts the same rupee. Mature marketplaces solve this by setting category-level CAC hurdles that vary with local fill rate, and by never reporting a platform-wide LTV-to-CAC ratio at all.

Regulated. In lending and insurance, the customer carries a loss distribution as well as a margin. A borrower's lifetime value is contribution net of expected credit loss, which is a vintage property, not a customer property — the same acquisition channel produces different credit quality in different quarters. Indian digital lending has made this vivid: the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending directions reshaped how sourcing costs can be borne and disclosed, and default-loss-guarantee arrangements moved risk back onto platforms that had modelled themselves as pure distributors. A CAC that does not net expected loss is not a conservative estimate; it is the wrong quantity.

Hardware plus software. Acquisition cost includes any negative-margin hardware, and payback becomes a working-capital question as much as a profitability one. A company adding 180 installs a quarter at ₹2,13,667 of effective CAC is putting ₹3.85 crore of cash out of the door every quarter before a rupee returns, of which ₹1.75 crore is device subsidy that will sit in the field for years. Growing that at 25 per cent a quarter compounds the cash requirement faster than the contribution stream can catch it.

AI-native. Three specific breaks. Cost to serve is variable and usage-linked, so gross margin is a customer-level property rather than a company-level constant — the heaviest decile of Pratyush AI's users ran at 41 per cent margin while the lightest ran at 74 per cent, and the blended 62 per cent described nobody. Churn is often not a binary event but a continuous contraction of usage, which makes "one divided by churn" undefined and forces a dollar-retention curve. And the observation window is short relative to the rate of change in the underlying technology, which means the truncation in convention F above is not conservatism — it is the only honest option.

Figure 3. The organisational seam is the real failure point. Four functions each control one term, each has a locally reasonable convention that happens to flatter their own performance, and the composite error is multiplicative rather than averaging out. A team that excludes growth salaries (overstating the ratio by ~20 per cent), counts organic conversions in a paid denominator (~60 per cent), uses gross rather than contribution margin (~15 per cent) and quotes month-twelve churn (~10 per cent) will report a ratio roughly 2.5 times the honest figure, with no single person having done anything wrong.

How do mature companies actually handle this, as opposed to how they describe it? Almost universally by keeping two sets of books. There is a board-facing blended ratio, computed on a stable convention, whose function is longitudinal comparability rather than decision support — it exists so that the fourth quarter can be compared with the first. And there is an internal marginal payback hurdle, set by channel or segment, against which spend is actually released. The board number is rarely wrong; it is simply not the number anyone uses to decide anything. Practitioners who do not understand this distinction spend their careers confused about why the board deck says five-to-one while the growth team is being told to stop spending.

Section sixNine distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

1. Improving retention that is actually survivorship. The tell-tale sign is a churn rate that falls smoothly and monotonically across a period in which the company shipped nothing meaningful. The obvious reading — the product is getting stickier — is wrong because a mixed cohort's aggregate hazard declines mechanically as its worst members leave, as Figure 1 shows. The expert's check is to compare hazard at equal tenure across cohorts, not across calendar time. If month-three churn for the January cohort matches month-three churn for the July cohort, nothing has improved; the population has merely aged.

2. A CAC that improves whenever spend is cut. The tell-tale sign is a step improvement in reported CAC in the same month a budget was reduced. The obvious reading — the team removed waste — is wrong because conversions from prior, larger spend are still landing in the denominator while the numerator has already shrunk. The expert asks for CAC computed on cohort-matched spend, lagged by the median time-to-conversion, and treats the calendar-month figure as decoration.

3. The blended denominator contaminated by organic. The tell-tale sign is that the ratio of new customers to paid spend improves as the brand gets better known. The obvious reading — efficiency — is wrong because word of mouth is being credited to the performance-marketing budget. The expert's diagnostic is a single question: if we switched off all paid spend for a month, how many customers would still arrive? Whatever that number is, it belongs out of the denominator and, ideally, in a separate line with its own cost structure.

4. Payback and LTV-to-CAC cannot both bind. The tell-tale sign is a business that clears both thresholds comfortably and is nonetheless told to spend less. The obvious reading — the CFO is being irrational — is usually wrong. Payback is a cash-and-capital constraint; the ratio is a value constraint. Which one binds depends on cost of capital and access to it. A well-capitalised company in a growing market should accept a long payback and a modest ratio; a cash-constrained company should refuse a short payback if the ratio is thin. The expert's habit is to ask which constraint the company is actually operating under before quoting either number.

5. Gross margin is not a constant, and averaging it destroys the analysis. The tell-tale sign is a single company-wide margin percentage applied to every cohort. The obvious reading — it is close enough — is wrong wherever cost to serve correlates with the same characteristics that drive acquisition. Cheap customers usually cost more to serve: discount-seekers use more support, free-trial converts use fewer features and ask more questions, and in AI products the highest-usage accounts carry the lowest margin. The expert computes margin at cohort or segment level and is unsurprised when the cheapest channel turns out to be the least profitable.

6. The discount rate is doing the work. The tell-tale sign is a lifetime value figure that is large relative to annual contract value in a business with net revenue retention above 100 per cent. The obvious reading — expansion is valuable — is true but incomplete; the specific magnitude is entirely an artefact of the discount rate, because the underlying series barely converges. The expert never presents such an LTV without the rate stated and a sensitivity beside it, and generally prefers a truncated-horizon figure that does not depend on the rate at all.

7. Strategic accounts are not exempt from arithmetic; they have different arithmetic. The tell-tale sign is a large deal waved through on the word "logo" or "lighthouse." The obvious reading — that this is an abandonment of discipline — is too quick. The honest version models the second-order benefit explicitly: if a marquee reference genuinely shortens the sales cycle for the next twenty deals by three weeks each, that is a computable reduction in future CAC and can justify an extraordinary acquisition cost. What is not defensible is claiming the benefit without ever measuring whether the reference was used.

8. Marginal CAC is a curve, not a number. The tell-tale sign is a plan that assumes doubling spend doubles customers. The obvious reading — that the channel is "working" — ignores that every acquisition channel has a saturation profile, and the marginal cost of the next customer rises as the addressable pool within that channel is consumed. The expert's habit is to ask for CAC at the margin at three spend levels, not one, and to recognise that a channel with a flat marginal curve is far more valuable than a cheaper channel that saturates at a tenth of the volume.

9. Payback is a statement about a cohort, and cohorts have shapes. The tell-tale sign is a company reporting a single payback number for a business whose cohorts differ materially by geography, plan or channel. The obvious reading — that the average is representative — fails badly when the distribution is bimodal, which it usually is. A blended nine-month payback composed of a four-month enterprise cohort and a never-repaying self-serve cohort is not a nine-month business; it is two businesses, one of which should be shut and the other funded harder, and the average conceals both conclusions.

8.2 Prateek Exchange: two sides, and the temptation to count a rupee twice

Prateek Exchange, a Rajkot-based business-to-business marketplace for industrial fasteners and spares, connected roughly 4,200 supplier-fabricators to 18,000 buying micro, small and medium enterprises. Buyer acquisition cost was ₹6,800 fully loaded; a buyer transacted ₹1.9 lakh of gross merchandise value a year at a 7.5 per cent take rate, and after payment fees, logistics subsidy and receivable losses the contribution was ₹533 a month against 2.5 per cent monthly churn. Naive buyer lifetime value was ₹21,320, a 3.1-to-1 ratio and a 12.8-month naive payback; corrected for churn, true payback was 15.2 months. Supplier acquisition cost was ₹41,000, dominated by catalogue digitisation and photography, against ₹1,400 a month of direct contribution at 1 per cent monthly churn — a 3.4-to-1 ratio that looked adequate and entirely missed the point.

The point was cross-side. Prateek's analysts established that buyers transacting in categories where the fill rate exceeded 82 per cent churned at 1.6 per cent a month rather than 2.5 per cent, which raises buyer lifetime value from ₹21,320 to ₹33,313 — an uplift of ₹11,993 per buyer. In an under-supplied category with twenty-six active buyers, adding one supplier that lifts fill rate past the threshold is worth more than ₹3 lakh of buyer value, against a supplier acquisition cost of ₹41,000. The correct policy is therefore a supplier CAC hurdle that varies by category fill rate, running as high as ₹2 lakh in thin categories and as low as ₹15,000 in saturated ones. The error waiting at the end of this reasoning is to credit the uplift to the supplier and simultaneously report buyer lifetime value at ₹33,313 in the board pack. Prateek did exactly that for two quarters, producing a platform-level valuation that counted the same retention improvement on both sides of the ledger.

8.3 Pratyush Learning: the failure, and what recovery actually looked like

Pratyush Learning sold an online entrance-examination preparation course at ₹41,000 a year, largely financed through nine-month instalments arranged with a non-banking financial company partner. Through financial year 2024 the company reported an acquisition cost of ₹4,900 and a lifetime value of ₹55,350, computed as the ₹41,000 course price multiplied by an assumed 1.35 courses per student. The ratio was 11.3-to-1. The board tripled the marketing budget.

Four errors compounded. Lifetime value was computed on revenue, not contribution; after content amortisation, allocated faculty cost, doubt-resolution staffing and payment and subvention fees, contribution margin was 54 per cent. Revenue was recognised at enrolment while cash arrived over nine months, and 11 per cent of instalment contracts defaulted, with the loss borne by Pratyush under a first-loss default guarantee. Fourteen per cent of students exercised the cooling-off refund. And the 1.35 repeat multiple was extrapolated from the first 200 students, a self-selected group of early adopters; the realised multiple across 40,000 students was 1.06. Finally, 38 per cent of enrolments were organic or referral but sat in the denominator against paid-only spend, so true paid acquisition cost was ₹4,900 ÷ 0.62 = ₹7,903.

Recomputed honestly: contribution per enrolment of ₹41,000 × 0.54 = ₹22,140, reduced by refunds to ₹19,040, reduced by expected instalment losses to a realised ₹13,600, multiplied by 1.06 for repeat, gives a lifetime value of ₹14,416 against a CAC of ₹7,903 — a ratio of 1.82-to-1, not 11.3-to-1, and a cash payback of roughly eleven months against an acquisition cost paid entirely in month zero. The company burned ₹62 crore over five quarters before the discrepancy surfaced in a cash-flow variance that the accounting-basis model could not explain.

The recovery took fourteen months and looked nothing like a model correction. The finance and product organisations rebuilt reporting on a cash-realised cohort basis, so a cohort was not counted as contributing until its nine months of instalments had cleared. The instalment channel with the default guarantee was replaced by a three-month part-payment scheme, which cut enrolments 34 per cent and cut defaults to 3 per cent. Marketing was capped at a six-month realised-cash payback hurdle, which closed roughly 60 per cent of channels outright. And one product change did more than all the financial engineering: a compulsory diagnostic test before enrolment, which disqualified students whose preparation level did not match the course, cut refunds from 14 per cent to 6 per cent at a cost of 19 per cent of top-of-funnel volume. Revenue fell 41 per cent in the following year. Monthly cash burn fell from ₹4.1 crore to ₹65 lakh, and the company reached contribution positivity in month eleven. The instructive detail is that no one at Pratyush Learning had falsified anything; every number had been computed by a competent analyst using a standard formula.

Section nineFailure modes, their early warnings, and the cost of catching them late

The first failure mode is the flattering convention that hardens into policy. Its early warning is a definition change that coincides with a fundraise or a reorganisation. The diagnostic question is: has the formula in this cell changed in the last four quarters, and who approved it? Caught early, the cost is an afternoon of reconciliation. Caught late, the cost is a board that has made two years of capital-allocation decisions on a number that was never comparable with itself, which is what happened at Pratyush Learning.

The second is funding marginal spend against blended economics. The early warning is a widening gap between the reported payback period and the rate at which cash actually returns. The diagnostic is to ask for payback on the most recent 10 per cent of spend rather than on all of it. Caught early it costs a quarter of channel-level instrumentation; caught late it costs the runway, because the blended number will keep looking acceptable until the cheap channels are fully saturated and then deteriorate very suddenly.

The third is extrapolating a retention curve past the data. The early warning is a lifetime value figure whose implied horizon exceeds the age of the company. The diagnostic is: what is the longest tenure we have actually observed, and what fraction of our claimed lifetime value accrues after that point? Caught early, the fix is truncation. Caught late, the cost is a business model built on a tail that does not exist — the classic pattern in consumer subscription, where cohorts that looked like they would stabilise at 40 per cent retention keep decaying.

The fourth is ignoring the payback ceiling. The early warning is a rising CAC in a business with high churn, with no one checking the ratio of CAC to monthly contribution divided by churn. The diagnostic is the single division in Figure 2. Caught early, the channel is closed. Caught late, the company has acquired several cohorts that were mathematically incapable of repaying their acquisition cost, and no amount of subsequent retention work can recover them.

The fifth is optimising a metric that marketing controls. The early warning is a marketing team hitting its CAC target while total new customers stagnate. The diagnostic is an incrementality test on the two cheapest channels. Caught early, the budget is reallocated. Caught late, the company has spent two years buying customers who were already arriving, and the true cost is the growth that was never attempted elsewhere.

The sixth is mistaking a step cost for a variable one, which is Pushkar Devices' near-miss. The early warning is a plan in which CAC is assumed constant while volume changes materially. The diagnostic is to ask which costs in the numerator would actually fall next quarter if volume halved. Caught early, it reframes the decision; caught late, it produces exactly the inversion in Table 4 — a cost-reduction initiative that raises cost per unit.

Section tenWhere experts genuinely disagree

Four disagreements are live, and none of them is resolved by better arithmetic.

Should lifetime value be reported at all? The cash school's strongest form is not that LTV is imprecise but that it is epistemically contaminating: placed on a slide beside CAC, which is measured, a forecast acquires the authority of a measurement, and no amount of caveating survives the second time the slide is shown. The evidence is the consistency with which companies that reported strong ratios failed on cash. The position would be wrong if forecast lifetime value could be shown to predict realised cohort value out of sample with reasonable accuracy — which, in businesses with stable cohorts and long observation windows, it demonstrably can. The disagreement is therefore about which businesses you are in, and both sides are right about different ones.

Is the three-to-one rule a floor, a target, or noise? The steelman for treating it as a target is that a ratio far above three indicates systematic underspending: if each customer returns five times their cost, the company should be buying more of them until the marginal ratio falls toward the cost of capital. The steelman against is that the ratio is computed on a blended basis, so a high blended ratio is entirely consistent with a marginal ratio already below one — the average is being held up by organic customers who cost nothing. This position would be wrong if marginal and blended economics were close, which is true only in businesses with a single dominant channel. Almost nobody is in that position, which is why the rule survives as a screen and dies as an instruction.

Should payback be measured on gross margin or on contribution? The gross-margin camp argues for comparability: every SaaS company computes it that way, and a metric whose main use is benchmarking should not be redefined locally. The contribution camp argues that variable support, success and success-adjacent costs are real cash that the customer causes, and excluding them systematically flatters businesses with heavy service models. The camps are reconcilable in principle and never in practice, because the reconciliation requires agreeing which costs are customer-caused, and that argument is genuinely hard in a business where a customer-success manager covers forty accounts.

Does short payback discipline destroy value in winner-take-most markets? The option school's strongest evidence is a handful of famous cases — subscription commerce, streaming, category-defining platforms — where enforcing a twelve-month payback would have prevented the company from ever reaching the scale at which its economics inverted. The counter-evidence is the far larger set of companies that used exactly this argument and were simply wrong about whether their market had winner-take-most dynamics at all. The position would be falsifiable if there were a reliable ex-ante test for network effects strong enough to justify the deferral. There is not one, and the honest statement is that this disagreement is currently decided by judgement and by access to capital rather than by evidence.

Section elevenWhat mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this topic produces the numbers correctly and defends them. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four observable ways.

They ask what decision the number is for before computing it, and frequently discover that the decision is insensitive to the disputed quantity. Meera's contribution at Pushkar was not a better lifetime-value model; it was recognising that the price decision turned entirely on whether field sales cost was fixed or variable, and that no amount of precision elsewhere mattered.

They state their conventions unprompted. An expert presenting a payback figure says, in the same breath, whether it is naive or churn-adjusted, whether margin is gross or contribution, whether the denominator is attributed or incremental, and how many months of real cohort data sit behind it. This is not pedantry; it is the only way two people can disagree productively, because a disagreement about a number is unresolvable until both parties know it is really a disagreement about a convention.

They prefer observed facts to modelled ones wherever the fact exists. Cumulative contribution at day 365 is a fact. Lifetime value is a model. Where both are available, the expert leads with the fact and offers the model as context, which inverts the usual presentation order and is strikingly more persuasive to anyone who controls capital.

And they hold the framework loosely enough to notice when it is the wrong frame entirely. The question "can we afford to acquire this customer" presupposes that customers are acquired one at a time through spend. For a business whose growth comes from a distribution partnership, a regulatory change, or a product that spreads because it is worth talking about, the framework will produce impeccable answers to a question the business is not facing. Recognising that is the last thing anyone learns, and the hardest to teach.

Section twelveThe decisions, and three questions

Meera Iyengar recommended against the price increase and won, though not on the argument she started with. The board accepted Table 4's finding that raising the device price would raise effective acquisition cost, because the field organisation was a step cost. What the board did not accept was her fifteen-month payback as a permanent state: Sandeep Bhatia's constraint was real, and the compromise reached on 3 March 2026 was to hold the price, cap installations at 150 a quarter rather than growing them, and use the freed ₹64 lakh a quarter to fund the pre-qualification workflow. Pushkar chose to grow more slowly at a better cost per unit rather than faster at a worse one — a decision available only because someone had separated the two effects that the single word "CAC" had been hiding.

Rohan Malaviya did something narrower and arguably more consequential. He stopped reporting lifetime value at Pratyush AI entirely. In its place the board pack now carries three observed figures — cumulative contribution per acquired customer at twelve, twenty-four and thirty-six months, computed on realised margin at the actual per-customer inference cost — alongside a marginal payback by segment. The thirty-six-month figure, ₹13.9 lakh against a ₹9.5 lakh acquisition cost, is considerably less flattering than the ₹66.7 lakh that convention A had produced. Rohan's argument to his chief executive was that the company was about to raise capital, that the investors would discover the gap between conventions during diligence, and that the difference between finding it yourself and having it found for you was the difference between a credible management team and a repriced round.

Questions for discussion

One. Pushkar Devices' effective acquisition cost rose when it raised its device price. Under what conditions would the opposite have been true, and what would Meera have needed to know about her field sales organisation — before the pilot, not after — to predict which case she was in?

Two. Prateek Exchange's supplier acquisition is justified largely by buyer retention it enables. If you were setting the company's capital-allocation policy, how would you prevent the same rupee of value from being counted on both sides, and what would you give up by adopting the most conservative rule?

Three. Rohan Malaviya removed lifetime value from the board pack. His chief revenue officer argued that this understates a business with genuine expansion and will make the company look worse than a less disciplined competitor that reports convention A. Who is right, and does your answer change if Pratyush AI is raising capital in six months rather than twenty-four?

Section thirteenGoing deeper

Unit economics is the parent frame: CAC, LTV and payback are unit economics stretched over time, and the discipline of defining a unit precisely is what makes all three computable at all. SaaS metrics: ARR, MRR, churn and NRR supply the recurring-revenue vocabulary in which these quantities are conventionally reported, and reveal how net revenue retention above 100 per cent quietly breaks the standard lifetime-value formula. Modelling LTV from retention is the direct next step from Section 3.1: it replaces the scalar churn rate with an observed survival curve and introduces the probabilistic models that handle heterogeneity properly. Acquisition channels and economics unpacks the marginal-cost curve behind Section 3.4 and is where incrementality testing actually gets done. Metrics by funnel stage decomposes acquisition cost into the conversion rates that produce it, which is the only way to know whether a rising CAC is a traffic problem or a conversion problem. Cohort-level P&L and payback curves turns the payback number into the forecasting instrument that Pratyush Learning's recovery depended on. Blended versus marginal economics is the single distinction that resolves most disagreements about these metrics and deserves study in its own right. Reading a P&L and gross margin and cost to serve together determine whether your margin input is honest; contribution margin is the specific quantity Section 3 argues should replace gross margin in every payback calculation. Cash flow, burn and runway supplies the constraint that made Sandeep Bhatia's objection legitimate rather than merely conservative. Market sizing (TAM / SAM / SOM) matters because a channel's marginal CAC curve is ultimately bounded by the size of the addressable pool, and Fermi estimation is the skill that lets you sanity-check any of these numbers in the ninety seconds before someone presents them to a board.
