ARR, MRR, Churn and NRR: Four Conventions That Choose a Company's Strategy For It

The mechanics of subscription metrics are arithmetic a schoolchild could do. The difficulty lies one level up: every one of these numbers rests on a definitional choice that is not forced by the facts, and the choice a company makes quietly determines how much growth it will be obliged to buy each year. This page is about that second level.

1. Two rooms, five weeks apart

On the morning of 11 November 2026, in a glass-walled room on the fourth floor of an office block off Bengaluru's Bellandur lake, Aparna Sundaram was asked a question she had been dreading for six weeks. Aparna was the vice-president of product at Nirjara Intelligence Cloud, a five-year-old company whose software read insurance claim files, loan application bundles and hospital discharge summaries, extracted the structured facts out of them, and pushed those facts into the core systems of insurers, non-banking financial companies and third-party administrators. Eighty-four enterprise accounts. A contract structure that had seemed elegant when the company designed it in 2023 and was now the single most contested item in a Series C data room: a fixed annual platform fee, plus a per-thousand-pages consumption charge above a contracted minimum.

The question, from a partner at the lead fund who had spent the previous week in the billing data, was flat and unhelpfully simple. “What is your ARR?” Aparna had two defensible answers and no way to give both without appearing to hedge. The first was ₹38.6 crore — the sum of platform fees and contracted consumption minimums across all live agreements, the amount Nirjara would collect over the next twelve months if every customer did precisely nothing more than it had already committed to in writing. The second was ₹61.2 crore — October's actual recurring billings of ₹5.10 crore, annualised, the amount Nirjara was in fact earning at its current run rate. The gap between them, ₹22.6 crore, was not an accounting error. It was uncommitted consumption: real revenue, invoiced and collected, arising from customers processing more documents than they had promised to process, and cancellable by those customers at any time without breaching anything, without a notice period, and without ever appearing in a churn report as a lost logo.

Aparna's difficulty was that the two numbers implied two different companies. At ₹38.6 crore of committed ARR, Nirjara's net revenue retention was a respectable 104 per cent and it was a solid mid-market software business. At ₹61.2 crore of consumed ARR, its net revenue retention was 128 per cent and it was the kind of company that gets a premium multiple. Both statements were true of the same eighty-four customers on the same Tuesday. The partner was not trying to trap her; he genuinely did not know which number to put in his investment committee memo, and he had asked because he wanted her to tell him which one she managed the business against. Aparna realised, somewhere in the pause before she answered, that she did not have a settled view — and that this, not the number itself, was the real finding of the diligence.

Five weeks later and nine hundred kilometres north-west, on 16 December 2026, Ritwik Barua was having an argument in Vadodara that looked nothing like Aparna's and was, underneath, exactly the same argument. Ritwik was chief product officer at Nikhil Grid Systems, which made smart electricity meters and the head-end and meter-data-management software that turned the readings from those meters into billing, outage and theft-detection workflows for state distribution utilities and large industrial estates. Nikhil had just won a tender: 2.4 lakh meters for a state discom, a seven-year term, total order value ₹41.2 crore. The chief executive wanted to announce that the win had added ₹5.89 crore to ARR — ₹41.2 crore divided by seven — and the chief financial officer had told him, in writing, that she would not sign a board pack containing that sentence.

Ritwik's position was that they were both wrong in an interesting way. The tender bundled four economically distinct things: hardware, a one-time installation and commissioning programme, a seven-year software subscription, and a six-year annual maintenance contract. Under Ind AS 115, the company would have to allocate the ₹41.2 crore across those performance obligations by their standalone selling prices anyway for statutory reporting; the same allocation, Ritwik argued, was the only honest basis for an ARR claim. On that basis the win added ₹1.40 crore of software ARR — not ₹5.89 crore — plus ₹0.75 crore a year of maintenance revenue at roughly half the gross margin, and ₹26.9 crore of revenue that was not recurring at all, however many years it took to deliver. And at the end of year seven the contract would not renew or churn in the way a SaaS contract does; it would go back to competitive tender, which is not a hazard rate but a coin toss with a date on it.

Aparna and Ritwik had, between them, encountered every serious problem in subscription metrics. Neither had an arithmetic problem. Both had a problem of convention — and conventions, as this page will argue, are not neutral. The convention a company adopts for what counts as recurring, which customers sit in the retention denominator, and whether a price escalation is expansion, does not merely describe the business. Through the identity that binds these numbers together, it determines how much of next year's growth the company will be forced to buy in the market rather than harvest from the customers it already has.

2. The idea: an annualisation convention, its history, and four schools that will not agree

Begin with precision, because the looseness starts early. Monthly recurring revenue is the normalised monthly value of the contractual obligations currently in force, irrespective of billing schedule or revenue recognition. Annual recurring revenue is that figure multiplied by twelve, or in some houses the normalised annual value of contracts in force, which is the same thing arrived at from the other end. Neither is a measurement in the way that revenue under Ind AS 115 or IFRS 15 is a measurement; both are run-rate constructs, forward-looking assertions about a hypothetical steady state in which nothing changes. They have no statutory definition, no auditor's opinion attached, and no comparability guarantee across two companies. That is not a scandal — it is the price of a number that is available on the fifth of the month rather than the forty-fifth, and that describes the future rather than the past. But it means every argument about ARR is ultimately an argument about a policy, and policies are chosen by people with incentives.

The historical problem these constructs were invented to solve is worth recovering, because it explains their shape. Enterprise software before roughly 2000 sold perpetual licences with an annual maintenance stream attached, conventionally 18 to 22 per cent of licence value, which entitled the customer to patches and version upgrades. Revenue was therefore violently lumpy — a large licence closed in March flattered a year that was otherwise flat — and the maintenance stream, though genuinely recurring, was treated as an afterthought in valuation. When hosted and then subscription delivery arrived, the lumpiness inverted: a company could sign a contract worth more over its life than the old licence and book almost nothing this quarter. Investors needed a comparability device that let them place a ₹40,000-a-year contract and a ₹4-crore-a-year contract on the same axis and, more importantly, let them see the cumulative installed base rather than the quarter's noise. MRR and ARR are that device. They were formalised in practitioner writing through the 2010s — David Skok's essays gave many of the definitions their standard shape, and Bessemer Venture Partners' annual cloud reports standardised them on the investor side — and they entered the formal disclosure record through S-1 filings, where companies began publishing them as non-GAAP supplements with a definitions footnote that almost nobody read.

Net revenue retention arrived later and for a different reason. Through 2019 and 2020 a cohort of newly public software companies disclosed it in their filings — Snowflake's figure at the time of its 2020 listing, reported at around 158 per cent, became the canonical example — and analysts seized on it because it answered a question that growth rate could not: how much of this company's growth is it buying, and how much is it harvesting? The metric goes by at least four names in the wild (net revenue retention, net dollar retention, dollar-based net expansion rate, net retention), and the fact that four names coexist is itself evidence that no standards body ever settled it.

Underneath the vocabulary sit four positions that experienced practitioners actually hold and that genuinely conflict. It is worth stating each as a proposition its adherents would and would not sign.

The contract school holds that ARR is a contractual concept: only amounts a customer is legally obliged to pay over the next twelve months, net of any cancellation right, belong in it. It would sign: “A company's ARR should not include revenue a customer can stop generating tomorrow without breaching anything.” It would not sign: “Consumption above the committed floor is ARR because it has been stable for six quarters.” Its evidence is the behaviour of usage-based revenue in the 2022–2023 software spending contraction, when many companies' consumption fell sharply while their logo churn barely moved. Aparna's ₹38.6 crore is this school's number.

The run-rate school holds that ARR should describe what the business is actually earning now, because a floor that customers habitually exceed by sixty per cent is a floor, not a forecast. It would sign: “A metric that systematically understates current economics by more than a third is not conservative, it is wrong.” It would not sign: “Include a signed contract that has not yet begun billing.” Its evidence is that consumption businesses with high customer concentration in mission-critical workflows show usage patterns closer to a utility bill than to a discretionary purchase. Aparna's ₹61.2 crore is this school's number.

The cohort school, whose intellectual heritage runs through direct marketing and consumer subscriptions rather than enterprise software, holds that ARR and NRR are both lossy summaries of the only object that matters — the revenue survival curve of each acquisition cohort, discounted. It would sign: “NRR above 100 per cent is a statement about the shape of a curve, and you should show me the curve.” It would not sign: “A single blended company-level NRR is a sufficient description of retention health.” Its evidence is the routine discovery, in diligence, that a healthy blended figure is the average of a thriving large-account book and a decaying small-account book.

The reconciliation school, usually staffed by chief financial officers and auditors, holds that ARR is a non-GAAP metric whose only legitimate use is alongside a published definition and a reconciliation to recognised revenue. It would sign: “Any ARR number without a written policy document is an opinion, not a metric.” It would not sign: “ARR figures are comparable across two companies in the same category.” Its evidence is the definitional drift it observes inside its own companies every time a new revenue stream appears.

These four positions are not reconcilable into a synthesis, and the honest thing to say is that no synthesis exists. What exists is a defensible practice: pick a convention, write it down, apply it without exception including in quarters when it hurts, and disclose enough of the underlying components that a sophisticated reader can recompute the number under a different convention if they wish. That is what Aparna eventually did, and section twelve records what it cost her.

3. Mechanics in depth: the identity, the ceiling, and the sorting effect

The first thing an expert does with these four numbers is stop treating them as four numbers. They are bound by an identity that almost nobody writes down and that, once written down, reorganises how a product leader thinks about a roadmap.

Let A0 be ARR at the start of a period and A1 at the end. Let r be net revenue retention over that period expressed as a decimal, computed on the cohort of customers live at the start. Let N be ARR added from customers who were not live at the start. Then, by construction and not by approximation:

A1 = r · A0 + N, and therefore growth g = (r − 1) + N/A0

Read the second form slowly, because it contains the entire strategic content of the topic. A company's growth rate is the sum of exactly two terms: what its existing customers did to it, and how much new business it bought relative to its size. There is no third term. A board that wants forty per cent growth from a company running 96 per cent NRR is, whether or not anyone says so, demanding new ARR equal to 44 per cent of the starting base every single year — and since new ARR costs money to acquire, that demand converts directly into a sales-and-marketing budget and a payback period. The same board asking the same forty per cent from a company at 128 per cent NRR is asking for new ARR equal to just 12 per cent of base. Nirjara and a hypothetical peer at 96 per cent retention could report identical growth, identical revenue and identical headcount, and be separated by a factor of nearly four in how much acquisition machinery they must fund to stay there. This is why NRR, and not growth, is the number that moves valuation multiples: growth tells you the speed, NRR tells you the fuel consumption.

The identity has a second consequence that is less often drawn out. Hold N constant — a company whose sales capacity grows slowly, which describes most enterprise businesses — and the recursion At+1 = rAt + N has a fixed point whenever r < 1:

A∞ = N / (1 − r)

A company adding ₹12 crore of new ARR a year at 96 per cent net retention has a structural ceiling of ₹300 crore; the same company at 86 per cent retention has a ceiling of ₹85.7 crore and will spend a decade approaching it while its investors wonder why growth keeps decelerating despite a sales team that is hitting quota. Above 100 per cent retention the fixed point disappears and the series compounds without bound. The chart below plots the trajectories. It is, in the author's view, the single most useful picture in subscription economics, and it is almost never shown to product teams.

The second mechanic that separates experts from competent practitioners is knowing that the retention denominator is a choice, and that the choice moves the answer by more than most product decisions do. Consider Nirjara's second quarter of FY27 (July to September 2026). Seventy-nine accounts were live on 1 July, with combined starting MRR of ₹438 lakh. Over the quarter they generated ₹96 lakh of usage-driven expansion, ₹14 lakh of expansion from contractual price escalators tied to a wholesale price index clause that most contracts carried on their anniversary, ₹31 lakh of contraction, and ₹22 lakh of churn across four departing accounts. Of the ₹96 lakh of expansion, ₹37 lakh came from three accounts buying a different product — the claims-adjudication module, sold by a different team on a separate order form. Three conventions, all of them in live use at reputable firms, produce three answers.

Convention C restricts the cohort to accounts live at least twelve months, which removes eighteen younger accounts that carried a disproportionate share of the quarter's contraction and churn.

A fourteen-point spread, on one quarter, from one set of invoices. Nothing here is fraudulent; each convention answers a coherent question. Convention A answers “what happened to the revenue from last quarter's customers?” Convention B answers “is the product we sold them becoming more valuable to them?” Convention C answers “how do our mature relationships behave?” The expert's contribution is not to pick the right one in the abstract but to notice that Convention B, the least flattering, is also the one that would have told Nirjara something it did not already know: that stripped of index-linked price rises and of a cross-sell motion run by a different team, the core product's organic expansion was running at roughly break-even. That is a product finding. Conventions A and C bury it.

There is a third mechanic, and it is the one that most often makes intelligent people draw a false conclusion from true data. Churn rates measured on a mixed population fall over time even when no underlying churn rate improves at all. This is a pure sorting effect: the high-churn segment is disproportionately removed from the population by its own churning, so the survivors are increasingly drawn from the low-churn segment, and the blended hazard drifts downward. Take a thousand accounts, six hundred of them small businesses churning at five per cent a month and four hundred enterprises churning at half a per cent a month, and hold both hazards perfectly constant forever.

Two operational consequences follow. First, any company whose acquisition mix is shifting — and every company's mix shifts — must read churn by segment and by cohort or it will misread its own progress, in either direction. A company moving upmarket will see blended churn improve for reasons that have nothing to do with the product; a company opening a self-serve tier will see it worsen for the same non-reason. Second, the same effect runs through NRR, which is why comparing this year's NRR to last year's without holding segment mix constant is closer to astrology than analysis.

Two further mechanics deserve a sentence each because practitioners routinely skip them. The quick ratio — gross additions divided by gross losses, or (new + expansion) / (contraction + churn) — compresses the same waterfall into one efficiency number; Nirjara's Q2 figure was (68 + 110) / (31 + 22) = 3.4, which is respectable, and its virtue is that it cannot be flattered by growing the denominator. And gross margin converts ARR into a common currency. A rupee of Nirjara ARR carried 61 per cent gross margin because large-model inference costs sat in cost of goods sold; a rupee of conventional application-software ARR carries 78 to 82 per cent. Nirjara's ₹61.2 crore of consumed ARR was therefore worth about ₹37.3 crore of gross profit, where a same-sized traditional peer would carry roughly ₹49 crore. Treating the two as equivalent inputs to a valuation, or to a hiring plan, is a category error that the metric's own name invites.

4. When the framework applies, and when it actively misleads

The conditions under which ARR and NRR describe reality can be stated as four testable claims. They are worth applying to the protagonists rather than asserting in the abstract.

Claim one: revenue arises from a standing contractual obligation rather than a repeated purchase decision. For Nikhil's software layer this holds cleanly — the discom cannot stop paying the head-end subscription without terminating the contract. For Nirjara it holds only up to the committed floor; above it, every month is a fresh purchase decision made by an operations manager watching a cost line. This is exactly why the ₹22.6 crore gap is not merely a labelling dispute. Revenue that is re-decided monthly should not carry the word “recurring” without qualification.

Claim two: the churn hazard is approximately stationary within a cohort after an onboarding period. This is the assumption that makes annualising a monthly rate, or extrapolating a run rate, meaningful at all. It holds tolerably for Nirjara. It fails completely for Nikhil, whose revenue does not decay at a rate but terminates at a date: at the end of year seven the discom must re-tender under public procurement rules, and the hazard function is a spike, not a plateau. Applying NRR language to that book produces numbers that are arithmetically valid and behaviourally meaningless.

Claim three: expansion is structurally available inside the account. Seats, modules, usage tiers or volume must exist as things the customer can buy more of without a new procurement cycle. Nirjara passes emphatically. Nikhil passes weakly — meter count is fixed by the tender, and expansion arrives only through a scope amendment, which is a sale, not an upsell. A consumer subscription with one plan and one price fails outright, and for such a business NRR is bounded above by 100 per cent by construction, which makes benchmarking it against B2B figures meaningless.

Claim four: the price of a unit is stable in the currency of measurement. Index-linked escalators, foreign-exchange exposure on dollar-denominated contracts, and regulator-approved tariff revisions all break this. Nikhil's maintenance line escalated with a published index; Nirjara invoiced three Gulf and Singapore accounts in dollars. In both cases NRR silently absorbs a macro variable and reports it as customer behaviour.

Where the framework is not merely inapplicable but actively misleading is worth naming plainly. It misleads when the account base is small enough that one customer dominates the denominator — at forty accounts, an NRR quoted to one decimal place is theatre. It misleads during a platform migration, where moving customers to a new SKU registers as simultaneous churn and new business, flattering the acquisition number and destroying retention, with no economic event having occurred. It misleads when a company has just pushed a list-price increase through its base, producing an NRR spike that looks like product-market fit and is in fact a one-off transfer that also raises the probability of churn at the next renewal. And it misleads in any business where the customer relationship is real but the revenue is transactional — a payments company, a marketplace, a lender — where ARR can be constructed but describes nothing anyone would act on.

5. Hard edges: multi-product, two-sided, regulated, hardware-plus-software, AI-native

The seams are where the definitions break, and the seams are almost always organisational before they are conceptual.

Multi-product. When a company sells two products, the classification of a cross-sell decides two numbers at once. Call it expansion and NRR rises while customer acquisition cost per new logo falls, because the cross-sell's selling expense sits against no new logo. Call it new ARR and NRR falls while CAC rises. Nirjara's ₹37 lakh of claims-module sales in Q2 moved NRR by 8.4 points depending on which box it went into, and the two teams involved each preferred the box that flattered them. Mature companies resolve this with a written rule — typically: same legal entity, new order form, separately priced product is expansion for retention purposes but is credited as new bookings for compensation, with the two reconciled in a footnote — and then defend the rule against quarterly renegotiation, which is the hard part.

Two-sided and marketplace businesses. Here ARR usually should not be constructed at all. Take rate on gross merchandise value is not recurring in the contractual sense; it is a commission on a volume that both sides re-decide continuously. Companies that report “ARR” on marketplace take rate are annualising a transaction stream, and the correct metrics are cohort GMV retention on each side, liquidity, and take-rate stability. The exception worth knowing is the hybrid: a marketplace that also charges sellers a fixed subscription for tools. That subscription genuinely is ARR, and disclosing it separately from take rate is the mark of a company that understands its own business.

Regulated environments. Nikhil's customers are state distribution utilities whose tariffs are approved by state electricity regulatory commissions; its insurance-sector cousins sell into entities supervised by the IRDAI, and its financial-services cousins into entities supervised by the RBI. Three specific effects follow. Contract terms are often set by tender documents rather than negotiated, so packaging levers that drive expansion elsewhere are simply unavailable. Payment cycles are long and partly outside the customer's control, so ARR and cash decouple more than in commercial markets. And termination-for-convenience clauses, common in public procurement, mean the committed portion of ARR is legally thinner than it appears — a point the contract school makes with some force.

They do not blend. The reason is not purity; it is that blending destroys the ability to forecast, because the two lines have different lag structures and wildly different margins.

AI-native products. This is where the framework is under the most active strain, and Nirjara sits in the middle of it. Three specific problems. First, consumption revenue has no contractual floor to anchor ARR, which is the dispute Aparna faced; the emerging practice, borrowed from cloud infrastructure, is to sell committed consumption — the customer commits to spend ₹X over a term, drawing down against it — and to report both the committed balance (in effect a remaining-performance-obligation figure) and the actual consumption run rate. Second, cost of goods sold moves with usage, so expansion that would be pure margin in a seat-based business is only 55 to 65 per cent margin here, and NRR flatters the economics relative to what it would mean elsewhere. Third, and least discussed, model-price deflation means the same workload costs less to serve each year; a company that passes this through sees revenue contraction that is not a loss of value, while a company that does not pass it through sees expanding margin and a rising probability that the customer renegotiates. Neither shows up correctly in a retention number.

6. Ten nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Expansion from price escalation is not expansion. Many enterprise contracts carry an anniversary uplift tied to an index or a flat three-to-five per cent clause. This lands in the expansion line and raises NRR without the customer having adopted anything further. The tell-tale sign is seasonality with no operational cause: NRR that rises in the same month each year, most visibly in April for companies whose Indian enterprise contracts renew with the financial year. The obvious reading — that the product is deepening in the account — is wrong, and the correction matters because escalator-driven expansion has the opposite risk profile: it raises price without raising value delivered, and it is the most common trigger of a competitive re-evaluation at renewal.

NRR and GRR moving apart is a message, not noise. Gross revenue retention counts only losses and is capped at 100 per cent; net retention lets expansion offset them. When NRR holds steady at 112 per cent while GRR slides from 91 to 85 per cent, the company is losing customers and hiding it behind growth in the ones that stay — a state that can persist for years and then break suddenly when the expanding accounts saturate. The tell-tale sign is a widening spread between the two lines on the same chart. Most boards are shown only NRR, which is precisely why sophisticated investors ask for GRR first.

Tenure filters make retention better exactly when onboarding gets worse. Restricting the NRR denominator to accounts live twelve months or more is common and often defensible; it also removes the cohort most likely to churn. If onboarding quality deteriorates, the new cohort churns early, never enters the denominator, and the reported NRR improves. The tell-tale sign is reported retention rising while first-year cohort survival falls — two curves that should move together and do not. The obvious reading is that the company is getting better at keeping customers; the truth is that it is getting worse at keeping them long enough to count.

Migration events masquerade as churn plus acquisition. When a company retires a legacy SKU and moves customers to a new one, the billing system typically terminates one subscription and creates another. Unless someone has instrumented a migration flag, the waterfall records a churn and a new logo, inflating gross additions and gross losses simultaneously and mangling NRR. The tell-tale sign is a month in which both new ARR and churned ARR spike together, with the quick ratio roughly unchanged. The cost of missing this is worse than cosmetic: sales compensation is paid on the phantom new business, and the retention alarm pulls customer-success resource toward accounts that never left.

The parent–child hierarchy decision changes the churn story entirely. A conglomerate customer with nine subsidiaries on separate order forms produces nine logos or one, depending on how the account hierarchy is modelled. Lose two subsidiaries and logo churn is 22 per cent under one model and zero under the other. The tell-tale sign is a high logo-churn figure sitting beside a low revenue-churn figure in an enterprise book — almost always the signature of subsidiary-level attrition inside retained relationships. Experts insist on knowing the hierarchy policy before reading any logo-churn number from an enterprise company.

ARR and cash are related only through billing terms, and the relationship is large. Two companies at ₹60 crore ARR growing at forty per cent, one billing annually in advance and one monthly, differ by roughly ₹12 crore in cash collected over the year — twenty per cent of ARR in interest-free float that funds hiring the other company must raise equity for. The tell-tale sign of trouble here is not in the cash line but in the deferred revenue balance: when deferred revenue stops growing in line with ARR, contract durations are shortening, and shortening durations are one of the earliest reliable predictors of a churn wave, usually preceding it by two to three quarters. Customers who are losing conviction ask for monthly terms before they ask to leave.

Not all ARR is the same currency, and gross margin is the exchange rate. A rupee of ARR at 80 per cent gross margin and a rupee at 55 per cent are different assets, yet both are added into the same headline. For AI-native products where inference dominates cost of goods sold, and for products with heavy managed-service components, the distortion is material. The tell-tale sign is an ARR line growing faster than gross profit for more than two consecutive quarters. The obvious reading is that the company is investing in growth; the correct reading is that it is selling an increasing share of a lower-quality product, and that the mix shift will show up in the valuation multiple long before it shows up in the growth rate.

Seat-based pricing imports the customer's business cycle into your retention line. If pricing is per employee, NRR moves with the customer's headcount, which moves with the customer's industry. A vendor to Indian IT services firms enjoyed spectacular net retention through the hiring boom and then watched it collapse without a single product decision changing. The tell-tale sign is NRR correlating more tightly with a sector employment index than with any internal engagement metric. The obvious reading is that the product became stickier and then less so; the truth is that the pricing metric was a bet on someone else's growth.

Annual contracts delay the churn signal by up to eleven months. In an annual-contract business the customer usually decides whether to renew within the first ninety to one hundred and twenty days of the term, based on whether the implementation delivered; the churn is recorded eight to eleven months later. Reading churn as a current-period signal in such a business is reading a decision made three quarters ago. The tell-tale sign is a customer-success organisation that is busiest in the last sixty days before renewal — the point at which the outcome has long been determined. Experts build leading indicators from usage decay, support-ticket sentiment and executive-sponsor turnover, and treat the renewal date as an accounting event rather than a decision point.

Published benchmarks are survivorship-biased upward, and by more than people assume. Median NRR figures from investor surveys and cloud reports are drawn from companies that were funded, that survived to be surveyed, and that chose to respond — and that were free to choose the flattering convention from Table 1. The tell-tale sign is a benchmark quoted without a sample definition. The practical correction is not to abandon benchmarks but to compare a company only against its own history on a frozen definition, and to treat cross-company comparison as directional at best. A board that demands the industry median NRR from a company selling to small businesses in a price-sensitive market is demanding a number that the market structure does not permit.

7. How this changes across product types and company stages

In consumer subscriptions the framework changes shape rather than degree. There is usually no expansion vector, so NRR is capped at 100 per cent and is not worth computing; the object of study is the cohort survival curve and its integral, and the operative distinction is between voluntary churn (the customer decided) and involuntary churn (the payment failed). The second of these is a large and under-managed line in India specifically. The Reserve Bank's e-mandate framework for recurring payments requires pre-debit notification and, above a threshold the central bank has revised upward over time, an additional factor of authentication at each debit; card-on-file tokenisation added a further re-authorisation step. The practical effect is that a materially higher share of Indian consumer subscription debits fail at renewal than in markets where a stored card simply charges, and a consumer product manager who does not have dunning and mandate-repair on the roadmap is leaving revenue on the floor that no amount of product improvement will recover.

In B2B mid-market the framework is at its most native: accounts are large enough to track individually, expansion vectors exist, and NRR is directly steerable through packaging and customer-success investment. In enterprise, two things change. Deal concentration makes every metric noisier — a single account can move blended NRR by five points — and contract length makes every signal slower. Enterprise companies compensate by reading remaining performance obligation and average contract duration alongside ARR, because those two together say more about the next eighteen months than the retention rate does.

Platforms and marketplaces mostly should not use this vocabulary, as section five argued, and the honest statement is that the difference is not one of degree: applying NRR to take-rate revenue produces a number that is arithmetically computable and behaviourally empty. Hardware-plus-software businesses should maintain the two-line disclosure Nikhil adopted. AI-native products face the genuinely unsettled version of the problem, and it would be dishonest to present a consensus where none exists.

Stage changes the reading as much as category does. At seed stage, with fewer than forty accounts, every one of these metrics is dominated by individual customers and should be replaced by a named list. At Series A, cohort curves become readable but NRR remains noisy; the useful discipline is to publish a definition before the numbers matter, because definitions written under fundraising pressure are always flattering. At Series B and C the law of large numbers starts to work, segmentation becomes both possible and necessary, and the risk shifts from noise to concealment — the blended number becomes stable enough to hide divergence beneath it. At scale and post-listing, the metric becomes a disclosure with legal consequences, definitions freeze, and the interesting work moves to the footnotes: which customers are included, how foreign exchange is handled, whether acquired ARR is restated into prior periods.

8. Three worked examples, including one that failed

Example one: Nirjara reconciles two ARRs instead of choosing between them

Aparna's eventual answer to the investor was structural rather than rhetorical. She proposed a three-line disclosure that Nirjara has used since: committed ARR of ₹38.6 crore, consumed run rate of ₹61.2 crore, and a consumption coverage ratio of 1.59 — consumed divided by committed — tracked by cohort. The ratio turned out to be the most useful of the three, because it decomposed. Accounts in their first year ran at 1.18; accounts in year three or later ran at 1.94. That single split reframed the business: uncommitted consumption was not a risk evenly spread across the base, it was a maturity effect concentrated in Nirjara's oldest and stickiest relationships, which materially strengthened the case that it was durable. Aparna also proposed — and this was the part that took three months to negotiate internally — that the commercial team's target shift from bookings to committed ARR, so that somebody was accountable for converting proven consumption into contractual floors at renewal. Over the following two quarters, 41 per cent of the gap was converted into committed minimums at renewal, at an average three per cent discount to the prevailing consumed rate, which was the price of turning a fragile rupee into a durable one.

Example two: Nikhil learns that its retention metric is a tender calendar

Ritwik's board eventually accepted the ₹1.40 crore software ARR figure, but the more consequential finding came from a question the chief financial officer asked afterwards: what has actually happened at re-tender? Nikhil had six contracts reach the end of their initial term since 2019. It had retained four and lost two, giving 67 per cent retention at the cliff — a catastrophic number by SaaS standards. But the four retained contracts had all expanded scope on renewal (more meters, added modules for theft analytics), so revenue retention across the six was 88 per cent. Neither number is a churn rate, and Ritwik's insight was to stop pretending otherwise. He replaced the retention slide with a renewal calendar: every contract, its expiry date, its current annualised software revenue, and a red-amber-green judgement on the re-tender. That exposed the actual risk, which was concentration: ₹3.8 crore of the ₹9.1 crore software ARR came up for re-tender inside an eighteen-month window in 2029–30. No retention percentage would have surfaced that. The product consequence was specific — a two-year programme to build switching cost through data history and integration depth, targeted at the three contracts in that window rather than spread evenly across the base.

Example three: Nilaya Learning, where the approach failed

Nilaya Learning was a Mumbai company selling vernacular professional upskilling — short courses in Hindi, Marathi and Telugu for sales, accounting and field-service roles — at ₹399 a month or a discounted annual plan. In its Series B deck, dated January 2026, it reported ARR of ₹48.2 crore and net revenue retention of 104 per cent. Both figures were arrived at honestly by people who had learned the vocabulary from B2B sources and applied it to a consumer business where it did not belong.

The ₹48.2 crore was October 2025 billings of ₹4.02 crore multiplied by twelve. October 2025 contained both the festive campaign and a large performance-marketing push; it was the highest-billing month in the company's history by a margin of 34 per cent over the second-highest. The 104 per cent NRR was computed on the subset of subscribers paying by card-on-file auto-renewal — 38 per cent of the base — because subscribers on UPI e-mandates whose mandates failed at renewal had been classified as “involuntary, pending recovery” and excluded from the denominator entirely. Involuntary failures were running at 4.1 per cent of the active base per month, and only 31 per cent were recovered within thirty days.

9. Failure modes, their early warnings, and the cost of catching them late

Definition drift. A new revenue stream appears — a managed-service retainer, a training package, a partner rebate — and somebody makes a judgement call about whether it is recurring, and that call never gets written down. Three years later nobody can reconstruct the history. The early warning is an inability to answer, in under a minute, the question “what is the exact rule for whether something counts?” The diagnostic question is: show me the ARR policy document, and show me the last date it was amended and by whom. Caught early, it costs an afternoon. Caught during diligence, it costs a restatement of every historical period, which is both expensive and, to an investor, a signal about everything else the company has not written down.

Annualising a peak. Nilaya's failure. The early warning is a run-rate figure whose source month is not stated on the slide. The diagnostic question is: what was the second-highest month in the last six, and how far below this one is it? A gap above fifteen per cent means the company is annualising noise. Caught late, as Nilaya discovered, it does not merely reduce the number — it converts a valuation conversation into a credibility conversation, and those are not recoverable in the same round.

Classifying involuntary churn as recoverable. Payment failures sit in a limbo state that is genuinely ambiguous for thirty days and not ambiguous at all after ninety. The early warning is a “pending recovery” bucket that grows monotonically. The diagnostic question is: of the accounts that entered the pending bucket six months ago, what percentage are paying today? If the answer is below half, the bucket is churn wearing a different label. The cost of catching it late is that the acquisition engine is sized against a base that does not exist.

Retention on a frozen or filtered denominator. The early warning is reported retention improving in a quarter when the support organisation reports rising escalations. The diagnostic question is: how many accounts are in the denominator, and what happened to the accounts excluded from it? Caught late, it means a company has spent two years believing its onboarding was adequate.

Letting compensation design the metric. When a sales organisation is paid on bookings, a customer-success organisation on renewals, and neither on net retention, the classification of every ambiguous event is decided by whoever files the paperwork. The early warning is the same customer event being recorded differently by two systems. The diagnostic question is: who gets paid more if this is called expansion rather than new business, and who decides? The cost of catching this late is a compensation restatement, which is the single most destructive administrative event a commercial organisation can experience.

Renewal-date concentration. Contracts signed in a single strong quarter renew in a single quarter forever. Nirjara had 41 per cent of committed ARR renewing between January and March because Indian insurers align to the financial year; a six-point slip in that quarter's gross retention would cost ₹95 lakh in one go. The early warning is a renewal calendar nobody has ever plotted. The diagnostic question is: what share of ARR renews in our single largest renewal month? Above fifteen per cent is a structural risk that should be managed by deliberately staggering terms at signature — a pricing decision, made years before the exposure appears.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether consumption revenue can be ARR at all. The contract school's strongest form is not pedantic: it observes that in the 2022–23 software spending contraction, companies with usage-based models saw revenue fall while logo churn stayed flat, which is precisely the failure mode the word “recurring” is supposed to warn you about, and that a metric which cannot warn you about its own principal risk is defective. The run-rate school's strongest form is that consumption in genuinely embedded workflows is more stable than seat counts in a hiring downturn, and that the contract school's conservatism is a bias toward the legally visible over the economically real. What would have to be true for the contract school to be wrong: uncommitted consumption in mission-critical workflows would have to show lower volatility than committed seat revenue across a full downturn, which is an empirical question with, so far, mixed evidence. What would have to be true for the run-rate school to be wrong: a single procurement-led cost review at a large customer would have to be able to remove a double-digit share of revenue without any contractual event — which it demonstrably can.

Whether NRR deserves its primacy. The case for is the identity in section three: NRR is the only variable that determines how much growth must be purchased, and it is therefore the correct summary statistic for capital efficiency. The case against is that NRR achieved through price escalation, seat inflation in a customer's growing business, or aggressive cross-sell attribution is not the same asset as NRR achieved through deepening product adoption, and that the metric's rise to primacy between 2019 and 2021 coincided so exactly with a valuation regime that rewarded it as to suggest the causation ran the other way. The sceptics' strongest evidence is the number of companies that reported NRR above 120 per cent in 2021 and below 105 per cent in 2023 without any product having got worse. What would have to be true for the sceptics to be wrong: NRR would have to predict forward three-year growth better than growth itself does, on a sample that includes the downturn — a test that is now finally possible to run and has not been run publicly at scale.

Whether gross or net retention should lead. A serious minority position holds that GRR should be the headline and NRR the supplement, because GRR cannot be flattered and measures the thing a product organisation actually controls: whether customers keep choosing to stay. Its evidence is that companies with strong NRR and weak GRR have repeatedly proved fragile once their expanding accounts saturated. The counter-position is that GRR penalises businesses whose model is land-and-expand by design, where early contraction is the expected cost of a low-friction entry point. What would have to be true for the GRR-first camp to be wrong: land-and-expand cohorts with weak first-year GRR would have to reliably converge to strong lifetime value — which happens, but far less often than the model's proponents assume.

Whether single-period metrics should exist at all. The cohort school's position is that MRR, ARR and NRR are all compressions of the cohort revenue surface, and that every compression discards the information a decision actually needs; the discipline should model discounted cohort revenue directly and treat the headline metrics as communication devices only. Its evidence is that every serious retention question resolves to a cohort question. The counter is practical: cohort surfaces cannot be governed, compensated against, or put in a credit agreement, and an organisation that cannot summarise cannot coordinate. Both sides are, in the author's judgement, correct about what they are defending, and the disagreement is stable rather than resolvable.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this topic can compute NRR from a waterfall. Someone who has internalised it does four things differently, and they are visible within about ten minutes of a metrics review.

First, they ask about the denominator before they react to the number. The reflex question — how many accounts, how many rupees, and what would this be if the largest one left — arrives before any judgement about whether 113 per cent is good. Second, they read pairs rather than singles: NRR beside GRR, ARR beside gross profit, retention beside average contract duration, growth beside new-ARR-as-a-share-of-base. They know that every one of these numbers has a partner that constrains its interpretation, and a slide showing one without the other reads to them as incomplete rather than as informative. Third, they convert metric findings into product decisions with a named mechanism. “NRR is down four points” is not a finding to them; “NRR is down four points, of which three come from contraction in accounts under two hundred seats, all of which reduced seats within sixty days of the new activation flow shipping” is. Fourth, and most distinctively, they are willing to argue for the less flattering convention in a room where a more flattering one is available, and to write the policy down before the quarter in which it will hurt. That last behaviour is the real marker, because it is the only one that costs something.

The four metrics do not measure a subscription business. They encode a set of choices about what the business will be held accountable for — and the identity A1 = rA0 + N then makes those choices binding, quarter after quarter, whether anyone noticed making them or not.

12. What they decided

Aparna took the three-line disclosure to Nirjara's board on 3 December 2026 and led with the committed figure, not the consumed one. Her argument was that Nirjara would be measured against whichever number it chose for the next four years, and that choosing the larger one would commit the company to defending a rupee it did not control. The consumption coverage ratio, broken by cohort, was the evidence that the uncommitted revenue was durable; the commercial target change was the mechanism that would make it contractual over time. The fund's investment committee memo used ₹38.6 crore of committed ARR, noted the ₹61.2 crore run rate, and valued the company on something between the two — which is, Aparna observed afterwards, exactly what would have happened anyway, except that she had chosen the frame rather than defended one.

Ritwik replaced Nikhil's retention slide with a renewal calendar, published an ARR policy that recognised only the software subscription line, and disclosed installed meters under management as the growth indicator alongside it. He lost the internal argument about the headline number in the press release — the company announced the ₹41.2 crore order value, as every infrastructure company does — but won the one that mattered, which was that the board pack and the investor materials carried ₹1.40 crore of added software ARR, and the 2029–30 re-tender concentration became a funded roadmap programme rather than a surprise.

Discussion questions

1. Aparna could have reported the ₹61.2 crore consumed run rate with a footnote disclosing the committed floor, rather than the reverse. Both disclosures contain the same information. Does the ordering change anything real, and if so, what is the mechanism by which a presentational choice becomes an operating constraint?

2. Nikhil's software ARR is ₹1.40 crore a year on a ₹41.2 crore order, and its retention at re-tender is 67 per cent by logo and 88 per cent by revenue on a sample of six. Is a subscription-metrics vocabulary the right one for this business at all — and if not, what should its board be reading first instead?

3. Nilaya's restated business was healthier than the one it had described, and was valued at less than half. Was the repricing a rational response to new information about the business, or to new information about the management team — and which of those two would you have been pricing if you had been in the room?

13. Going deeper

CAC, LTV and payback. The identity in section three makes new ARR the residual a company must buy; this topic prices that purchase and tells you whether the growth rate a board is demanding is affordable at all.

Revenue recognition basics. Ind AS 115 and IFRS 15 govern the statutory number that ARR is not; understanding allocation across performance obligations is what let Ritwik defend ₹1.40 crore against ₹5.89 crore.

B2B product metrics. Retention is a lagging indicator by construction; this topic supplies the leading ones — activation, depth of use, breadth of seats — that let you see a churn wave two quarters before it lands in the waterfall.

Subscription economics. The composite scores — Rule of 40, quick ratio, burn multiple, magic number — that boards use to rank companies against one another, and the specific ways each can be gamed.

Renewals, churn and NRR. The operational discipline underneath the metric: renewal forecasting, the health-score machinery, and why the renewal decision is usually made in the first quarter of the term rather than the last.

Reading a P&L. ARR never appears on one. Knowing where recognised revenue, deferred revenue and contract assets actually sit is what lets you spot the gap between a run rate and a result.

Gross margin and cost to serve. The exchange rate that converts ARR into comparable currency, and the topic that decides whether AI-native ARR is worth what seat-based ARR is worth.

Contribution margin. Pushes the margin question down to the segment and the account, which is where the Table 1 problem of blended figures hiding divergent segments finally gets resolved.

Unit economics. Assembles retention, margin and acquisition cost into a per-customer model — the thing the best programmes make teams build in a spreadsheet rather than hear about in a lecture.

Cash flow, burn and runway. The nuance in section six about billing terms and deferred revenue becomes a survival question here: two companies at identical ARR can have eleven months of runway between them.

Market sizing (TAM / SAM / SOM). The ceiling N/(1 − r) is an internal limit; market size is the external one, and a company should know which of the two it will hit first.

SaaS Metrics: ARR, MRR, Churn, NRR

What numbers will a board or investor read first for a subscription product — and what does a product manager need to know about them before she is the one presenting the slide?

A Tuesday in Gurugram, three weeks before the board meeting

Rhea Kapoor found the discrepancy on a Tuesday evening in August 2026, forty minutes before she was supposed to leave for a wedding reception. Rhea was the head of product at Saanvi Cloud Systems, a six-year-old Gurugram company that sold HR and payroll software to mid-market Indian manufacturers and logistics firms — the kind of customer that ran three hundred to four thousand employees, still reconciled provident-fund filings by hand, and paid Saanvi between ₹40,000 and ₹6 lakh a year depending on headcount and modules. The company had just closed its Series B eighteen months earlier and was now preparing the data room for a Series C, and the board meeting on 2 September was the one where the finance team would present the metrics that mattered most to that raise.

The discrepancy was this: the VP of Sales had told the CEO that the quarter had been the best in company history, citing ₹54 lakh of "new bookings." The CFO's spreadsheet, meanwhile, showed monthly recurring revenue had grown by only ₹12 lakh over the same three months. Both numbers were true. They were also answering different questions, and if Rhea could not explain the gap in the boardroom, the investors sitting across the table — two of whom ran the numbers for a living and would ask before anyone else could speak — were going to conclude that Saanvi's product leadership did not understand its own unit economics. That conclusion, more than any single bad number, was what killed valuations. Rhea's task over the next three weeks was to learn to read the same numbers the board would read, in the same order they would read them, well enough to explain not just what they said but what they could not say.

The idea: four numbers that describe a subscription business at any instant

Monthly recurring revenue (MRR) is the revenue a subscription business can count on receiving, on a normalized monthly basis, from the customers currently under contract — a ₹12-lakh annual contract counts as ₹1 lakh of MRR regardless of whether the customer paid in one instalment or twelve. Annual recurring revenue (ARR) is simply MRR multiplied by twelve; it is the same fact restated at the cadence boards and investors actually think in. Churn is the rate at which existing recurring revenue disappears — customers who cancel, downgrade, or fail to renew — measured either in the number of customers lost ("logo churn") or in the revenue those customers represented ("revenue churn"). Net revenue retention (NRR) is the single most consequential of the four: it asks, of the cohort of customers who were paying you at the start of a period, what fraction of their revenue you are still collecting at the end of it, after accounting for the ones who expanded, the ones who shrank, and the ones who left — but deliberately excluding any brand-new customer won during the period.

These four ideas were not invented by a single economist in a single year the way, say, net present value traces to a known lineage in corporate finance. They crystallised gradually as venture capital moved from funding on-premise software licences to funding subscription software in the 2000s and 2010s, and investors needed a vocabulary that let them compare a company selling ₹500-a-month tools to one selling seven-figure enterprise contracts. David Skok, a Boston-based venture partner, published an influential 2013 essay, "SaaS Metrics 2.0," that gave many of these definitions their now-standard form; Bessemer Venture Partners' annual "State of the Cloud" reports did the same work of standardisation on the investor side. Net revenue retention specifically became a headline number only after 2019, when a wave of newly public SaaS companies — Zoom, Snowflake, Datadog among them — began disclosing it in their quarterly filings and analysts started using it to separate durable businesses from ones merely buying growth through discounting. The sentence Rhea needed to be able to say in the boardroom without sounding glib was this: "MRR tells you what we are worth right now; NRR tells you whether the customers we already have are making that number go up or down on their own, before we sell a single new logo."

How it actually works: the mechanics, step by step

The mechanics begin with a decision practitioners often skip past: choosing what counts as "recurring." A one-time implementation fee is not recurring revenue, even though it appears on the same invoice as the subscription; Saanvi's finance team had, for two quarters the previous year, folded onboarding fees into MRR before an external auditor flagged it, quietly inflating the number by roughly six percent. Once the recurring base is defined cleanly, MRR for any given month is built from five components, and the discipline of tracking each one separately — rather than only the net total — is what turns MRR from a single opaque figure into a diagnostic tool.

Start with starting MRR, the recurring revenue in force on the first day of the month. Add new MRR, the recurring revenue from customers who signed their first contract during the month. Add expansion MRR, the additional recurring revenue existing customers began paying — an upsell to a higher tier, an added module, more employee seats. Subtract contraction MRR, the recurring revenue existing customers stopped paying without leaving entirely — a downgrade, a seat reduction. Subtract churned MRR, the recurring revenue from customers who cancelled outright. The sum is ending MRR, which becomes next month's starting MRR. This is usually drawn as a waterfall, because a waterfall makes visible something a single growth percentage hides: two companies can report identical net MRR growth while one is healthy and the other is bleeding out of a leaky bucket that new sales happens to be refilling faster than it drains.

− Churned MRR (5 accounts cancelled)−11.0
= Ending MRR (31 Aug 2026)154.0

Two figures follow immediately. Ending ARR is 154 × 12 = ₹1,848 lakh, or roughly ₹18.5 crore — the number the term sheet would eventually reference. And net MRR growth for the month is (154 − 142) / 142 = 8.5 percent, which sounds respectable until it is decomposed, because that respectable-looking 8.5 percent is the residue of ₹27 lakh of gross additions (new plus expansion) fighting ₹15 lakh of gross losses (churn plus contraction). A board that only sees the net figure cannot tell a company adding cleanly from one adding fast and leaking almost as fast; Rhea's job was to show both.

Now the churn and retention arithmetic, which is where most of the confusion in the boardroom actually lived. Gross revenue churn rate is churned MRR divided by starting MRR: 11 / 142 = 7.7 percent for the month. Gross revenue retention (GRR) is the mirror image, counting only losses and capping at 100 percent: (142 − 11 − 4) / 142 = 127 / 142 = 89.4 percent. Net revenue retention (NRR) does what GRR does but also lets expansion offset the losses, and critically it is calculated only over the cohort of customers who were already paying on 1 August — the eleven new logos are excluded entirely, because NRR is asking a narrower and more diagnostic question: not "did the company grow," but "did the customers we already had grow with us." NRR = (142 + 9 − 4 − 11) / 142 = 136 / 142 = 95.8 percent.

An NRR below 100 percent means the existing customer base is shrinking even before a single new customer is signed; a business at that level is running on a treadmill, replacing lost revenue with new-logo revenue just to stand still. Saanvi's 95.8 percent was not alarming on its own — the widely cited benchmark from investor surveys such as those published by Bessemer and by SaaS-focused bankers is that 100 to 110 percent is solid for a mid-market B2B company, and figures above 120 percent are associated mostly with enterprise products sold on a seat- or usage-based model where expansion is structurally large. But 95.8 percent moving in the wrong direction, three weeks before a fundraise, was exactly the kind of number an investor would ask Rhea to explain unprompted.

The second pass shows why the underlying driver matters more than the headline figure. Suppose Saanvi's customer success team, alerted mid-month, managed to save two of the five churning accounts by fixing a payroll-compliance bug that had been driving cancellations — a plausible intervention, since Rhea's product team had already traced three of the five cancellations to that exact defect. Churned MRR falls from ₹11 lakh to ₹5 lakh; every other line is unchanged. Ending MRR becomes 142 + 18 + 9 − 4 − 5 = 160 lakh instead of 154 lakh — a ₹6 lakh swing, or roughly ₹72 lakh of annualised ARR, from fixing one bug. NRR becomes (142 + 9 − 4 − 5) / 142 = 142 / 142 = 100.0 percent exactly. That single recalculation was the moment Rhea's argument to the CEO stopped being about vocabulary and became about a roadmap: the compliance bug fix, not any sales initiative, was the highest-leverage item in the company's next sprint, because its effect showed up directly in the metric the board would scrutinise first.

The nuances a learner must sit with

Bookings, MRR, and cash are three different facts, not three names for one fact

A signed contract for ₹36 lakh over three years is ₹36 lakh of total contract value, ₹1 lakh of MRR, and however much cash the payment schedule actually releases this month — often less than ₹1 lakh if the customer negotiated a slow ramp. Sales teams are usually compensated on bookings, finance teams live in MRR, and the CFO watches cash separately again. The VP of Sales at Saanvi was not lying about the ₹54-lakh quarter; he was reporting total contract value on a handful of multi-year enterprise deals, and none of those deals had been mapped back to their monthly-equivalent contribution before the number reached the CEO.

Logo churn and revenue churn measure different risks

Losing forty small customers worth ₹5,000 a month each and losing one customer worth ₹2 lakh a month can produce the same revenue-churn figure while describing opposite businesses — one with a broad base absorbing normal attrition, the other dangerously concentrated in a handful of accounts. A learner who quotes only one of the two numbers, without saying which, has not really answered the question.

NRR is a retention metric, not a growth metric

Because NRR excludes new logos by construction, a company can have excellent NRR and still be shrinking overall if new-customer acquisition has stalled, or mediocre NRR and still be growing fast on the strength of new logos alone. The two numbers must always be read together; a board slide that shows NRR without also showing new-logo ARR added in the same period is showing half a picture, deliberately or not.

Blended metrics hide the story that cohort metrics tell

A single company-wide NRR figure averages together customers signed six years ago, who may be maturely expanded, with customers signed six months ago, who have not yet had time to expand or churn. Sophisticated boards ask for NRR broken out by cohort — customers grouped by the quarter they signed — and by segment, because a 96 percent blended NRR can conceal a 110 percent NRR among enterprise accounts sitting next to an 80 percent NRR among small accounts that are quietly walking out the back door.

The measurement period changes the number, and not by a rounding error

Monthly churn of 2 percent sounds small; compounded, it implies annual revenue retention of roughly (1 − 0.02)^12 ≈ 78.5 percent, a figure that would alarm any investor if presented directly. Practitioners must always state whether a churn or retention figure is monthly or annual, and must never silently multiply a monthly rate by twelve to approximate an annual one, since churn compounds rather than adding linearly.

Contraction is often the earliest warning sign, and it is the one teams track least carefully

A customer that downgrades before cancelling is usually giving six to twelve months of advance notice of the churn to come, yet many dashboards fold contraction into a generic "other" bucket or net it silently against expansion. Separating the two is the cheapest early-warning system a subscription business has, and it was, not coincidentally, how Rhea's team first noticed the payroll-compliance bug pattern before it became five outright cancellations.

NRR cannot tell you why, only that

The metric is a symptom, not a diagnosis. A falling NRR can be caused by a product defect, by a pricing model that under-charges for the value delivered as usage grows (so customers never need to buy more), by a competitor's launch, or by a customer-success team stretched too thin to spot at-risk accounts. Reading NRR correctly means treating it as the prompt for an investigation, never as the investigation's conclusion.

A high headline ARR can still be a fragile number

ARR is a run-rate, a snapshot annualised forward, not a promise; a company with ₹20 crore of ARR built on annual contracts up for renewal next month is in a structurally different position from one with the same ARR built on contracts with eighteen months left to run, even though the two companies' ARR slides would look identical on the day of the board meeting.

Consumer, B2B, and marketplace products — and small companies versus large ones

In consumer subscription products — a streaming service, a fitness app — MRR per customer is small and the customer base is large, so churn is usually analysed as a cohort survival curve (what fraction of January's sign-ups are still paying in June) rather than dollar-by-dollar, and expansion MRR is nearly absent because there is rarely a "seat" to add; a consumer product manager reads retention curves the way a B2B product manager reads NRR. In B2B products like Saanvi's, the unit of analysis is the account, MRR per customer is large enough to track individually, and expansion is a designed growth lever — more seats, more modules, higher usage tiers — so NRR is often the single most-watched number in the business, since it is directly steerable through packaging and customer success investment. In marketplace products, the picture fragments further, because there are two sides (buyers and sellers, or in Saanvi's adjacent world, employers and gig workers on a payroll-disbursal feature) and a single blended MRR figure can mask one side growing while the other churns; marketplace teams typically track take-rate and liquidity metrics alongside, or instead of, a pure recurring-revenue figure, because not all marketplace revenue is contractually recurring in the SaaS sense at all.

Company stage changes the read as much as product category does. At an early-stage company with forty customers, NRR is dangerously noisy — the loss or expansion of a single large account can swing the blended figure by five or ten points in a month, so early-stage boards should be reading logo-level detail, not a single percentage, and a founder who leads with a precise NRR figure off a base that small is usually communicating false confidence rather than insight. At a larger company with thousands of customers, the law of large numbers makes NRR stable enough to trend month over month with real statistical meaning, and boards increasingly ask for it segmented by cohort, geography and contract size precisely because the aggregate is stable enough to obscure divergence underneath it.

Common mistakes

The first mistake is reporting bookings as if they were MRR, the exact error that started Rhea's Tuesday evening. The symptom is a sales number and a finance number that never reconcile, quarter after quarter, with someone always explaining the gap after the fact rather than before. The underlying misunderstanding is treating "revenue we have contracted for" as identical to "revenue we can count on this month." The cheapest diagnostic is a single line added to every deal-closed notification showing its monthly-equivalent MRR contribution alongside its total contract value, so the two numbers are never seen apart.

The second mistake is computing NRR over too small or too recent a customer base and presenting it with false precision, such as a two-decimal NRR figure drawn from thirty accounts. The symptom is a metric that swings by ten or more points between board meetings with no operational story behind the swing. The underlying misunderstanding is applying a statistic designed for stable, large populations to a population still small enough that individual accounts dominate it. The cheapest diagnostic is to ask, before trusting any NRR figure: how many accounts and how many rupees of MRR sit in the denominator, and would this number change materially if the single largest account in it left tomorrow?

The third mistake is conflating churn measured in logos with churn measured in revenue, and switching silently between the two depending on which one looks better that quarter. The symptom is a churn figure that seems to contradict the revenue trend — "we only lost three customers but revenue churn was 9 percent" — without anyone flagging that the three were disproportionately large accounts. The cheapest diagnostic is to require both figures on every metrics slide, side by side, permanently, so neither can be selectively omitted.

The fourth mistake is treating a single company-wide NRR number as if it describes every part of the business equally, when a healthy blended figure can be the average of a thriving enterprise segment and a decaying small-business segment. The symptom appears months later, when the small-business segment has shrunk so far that even a strong enterprise NRR can no longer offset it. The cheapest diagnostic is a standing quarterly habit of segmenting NRR by at least one dimension — contract size, industry vertical, or sign-up cohort — even when nobody has yet asked for the breakdown.

What good looks like

Six months before Rhea's board meeting, a smaller Pune-based SaaS company called Saumya Ledger Systems, which sold compliance and bookkeeping software to chartered accountancy firms, had gone through a similar reckoning and come out the other side with a metrics discipline worth naming as a model. Saumya's head of product had insisted, over the objections of a sales team eager to report only bookings, on a monthly one-page metrics memo circulated before every leadership meeting: the MRR waterfall broken into its five components, gross and net revenue retention shown separately and by cohort quarter, logo churn and revenue churn both stated, and a short written note attributing that month's largest single driver of churn or expansion to a named product or process cause rather than left unexplained. When Saumya's NRR dipped from 108 to 101 percent after a pricing change increased resistance among their smallest accounts, the memo said so plainly in the same month it happened, rather than surfacing three quarters later as an unexplained trend; the team reversed the pricing change for the affected tier within six weeks, and NRR recovered to 106 percent by the following quarter. Saumya's investors did not need to ask where the number came from or what it meant, because the company had already told them, in the same document, before the meeting began. That is the target: metrics owned and explained by the team that produces them, not reconstructed under pressure the week before a board meets them.

What Rhea decided, and what to read next

Rhea's decision was not to hide the bookings-versus-MRR gap or to bury it in a footnote; she rebuilt the metrics memo along the lines Saumya had pioneered, presented both the ₹54-lakh bookings figure and the ₹12-lakh net MRR growth on the same slide with the waterfall between them, and paired the 95.8-percent NRR with a one-line explanation naming the payroll-compliance bug, the two accounts already saved, and the sprint scheduled to fix it for the remaining at-risk cohort before the next board cycle. The investors' first question in the meeting was, predictably, about the NRR trend; Rhea's answer took ninety seconds and ended with a roadmap item rather than an excuse, which was precisely the difference between sounding like someone who understood the business and someone who was still learning to read its numbers in the room. From here, the natural next readings are CAC, LTV and payback — the metrics that tell Rhea what it costs to acquire the new logos this page mostly set aside — and subscription economics more broadly, including the Rule of 40 and the quick ratio, which combine growth and retention into single comparative scores investors use to rank SaaS companies against one another.

MRR tells a room what the company is worth this month. NRR tells the room whether the customers already in the building are the reason that number is rising, before a single new logo is signed.

Two questions to sit with:

1. If your own product's NRR fell five points next quarter, could you say within a day which cohort, which segment, and plausibly which root cause was responsible — or would you first have to go build the report that could tell you?

2. Whose compensation plan in your organisation rewards bookings, and whose rewards net retention — and what does the gap between those two incentives predict about which number gets inflated first when a quarter is going badly?
