Fermi Estimation

How to reach a defensible number by Thursday, when the data warehouse won't be back until the following Monday.

On the morning of 14 September 2026, Rohan Mehta, VP of Product at Ganana Mobility, a Chennai-headquartered shared-EV-scooter operator running roughly 18,400 vehicles across nine Indian cities, opened his laptop to find the one query he needed answered greyed out. The company's data warehouse had been mid-migration to a new provider since the previous Friday, and the dashboards that normally told him how many scooters broke down on the road each month were unreadable until the vendor finished reindexing — an estimated ten more days. The board was meeting in forty-eight hours to decide whether to fund a ₹1.4 crore predictive-maintenance program: sensors on each scooter's battery and motor that would flag failures before a rider was stranded. The single number the board would ask for first — how many roadside breakdowns Ganana's fleet actually suffers in a year — was, for the next ten days, unknowable from any system he had access to.

Rohan had two honest options. He could tell the board the number was unavailable and ask them to wait, which would push the decision past the October fundraising close the CFO had flagged as the natural moment to lock in this kind of capital spend. Or he could construct the number himself, in an afternoon, from pieces he did know, and defend the reasoning rather than the data source. He chose the second path, and the tool he reached for — not a spreadsheet trick, but a specific discipline for reasoning under near-total data scarcity — is the subject of this page.

The idea

Fermi estimation is a method for producing a defensible order-of-magnitude answer to a quantitative question when you have little or no direct measurement of the thing itself, by breaking the unknown quantity into a chain of smaller quantities you can each estimate from something you genuinely know, then multiplying the chain back together. It is named for the physicist Enrico Fermi, who was known at Los Alamos in the 1940s for producing startlingly accurate estimates — most famously the yield of the first atomic bomb test in 1945, which he approximated by dropping torn scraps of paper and watching how far the shock wave blew them, arriving within a factor of two of the value later confirmed by instruments. The technique was popularized as a teaching exercise through problems like "how many piano tuners are there in Chicago," and it later became a fixture of case-interview and product-management hiring precisely because it tests a skill distinct from data analysis: the ability to reason to a usable number when no dataset exists yet.

The problem Fermi estimation was invented to solve is not "how do I get an exact number" but "how do I get a number good enough to act on, fast, when the alternative is no number at all." The single sentence Rohan could say in the boardroom without sounding glib is this: break the unknown into pieces you can each anchor to something real, multiply them, and trust the order of magnitude — not the decimal point. That sentence does two jobs. It signals that the number is a structured estimate, not a measurement pretending to be one, and it tells the board exactly how much confidence to place in it.

How it actually works

The mechanics have seven steps, and the ones practitioners skip in a hurry are usually the fourth and the sixth — the sanity bound and the explicit range — which is exactly what turns a guess into an estimate.

First, state the question as a single quantity with explicit units and a time window: not "how bad is our breakdown problem" but "roadside breakdowns per year, fleet-wide." Second, decompose that quantity multiplicatively into a short chain of sub-quantities, chosen so that each link is something a person could plausibly know or find out, rather than something that requires the same missing dataset. Third, anchor each link to a real reference — a number you have seen, a figure a colleague can recall from memory, a publicly known ratio — rather than inventing a plausible-sounding figure with no source. Fourth, sanity-check each link against an absurdity bound: a breakdown probability of 1-in-10 would mean one in ten rides fails, which nobody at Ganana has ever reported, so that bound is easy to rule out. Fifth, multiply the chain through, tracking the order of magnitude (the power of ten) separately from the leading digits, since the power of ten is usually the part you can trust and the leading digits are decoration. Sixth, report the answer as a range — Fermi's own estimates were understood to be "within a factor of two," and a modern business version is usually a three-to-four-fold band around a central guess — rather than a single figure that invites false confidence. Seventh, identify which link in the chain the final answer would move the most for, and spend any remaining hours narrowing that one link rather than polishing the others.

A worked example

Rohan's first link, fleet size, needed no estimation — 18,400 active vehicles was a figure the finance team had confirmed for August's board pack days before the migration. His second link, trips per vehicle per day, he recalled from a utilization dashboard he had screenshotted in July for an unrelated slide: 4.2 rides per vehicle per day, fleet-wide average. His third link, operating days per year, he built from the calendar: 365 days minus roughly fifteen days of monsoon-related depot closures and scheduled battery-swap downtime, giving 350. His fourth and hardest link — the probability that a given trip ends in a roadside breakdown — he did not have a system number for at all, so he called three city operations leads. Each recalled, independently, roughly two breakdown-pickup calls per day for a city zone of about 2,000 active vehicles; at 4.2 trips per vehicle per day that zone runs about 8,400 trips a day, so two breakdowns against 8,400 trips is close to 1 breakdown in 4,000 trips — Rohan rounded this to a conservative 1 in 3,000 to avoid understating the case.

Table 1. Base-case arithmetic, worked line by line.
StepCalculationResult
Trips per day, fleet-wide18,400 vehicles × 4.2 trips/vehicle/day77,280 trips/day
Trips per year, fleet-wide77,280 × 350 operating days27,048,000 trips/year
Breakdowns per year, central case27,048,000 ÷ 3,000≈ 9,016
Breakdowns per year, if rate is 1-in-2,00027,048,000 ÷ 2,000≈ 13,524
Breakdowns per year, if rate is 1-in-5,00027,048,000 ÷ 5,000≈ 5,410

The central estimate — about nine thousand roadside breakdowns a year, or roughly twenty-five a day across the fleet — was already a striking number to bring into a room that had never seen it stated plainly. But Rohan ran a second pass before he trusted it. What if the utilization figure, 4.2 trips per vehicle per day, was stale, and tier-2 cities were actually running closer to 3.0 because of lower rider density? Substituting 3.0 for 4.2 changes the daily total to 55,200 trips, the annual total to 19,320,000, and the central breakdown estimate to 6,440 — a drop of just under 30%, exactly proportional to the drop in the utilization figure, because every link in a pure multiplicative chain moves the answer by the same percentage it itself moves.

That proportionality is the useful discovery from the second pass. Because every factor in the chain has equal leverage on the final answer in percentage terms, the link worth spending scarce hours narrowing is not the one that "feels" most uncertain but the one whose plausible range is widest. The utilization figure Rohan used ranges perhaps 3.0 to 4.2 trips per day — a band of about 40%. The breakdown-rate figure ranges from 1-in-2,000 to 1-in-5,000 by his ops leads' own accounts — a band of roughly 150%. The breakdown rate, not the utilization figure, was therefore the input worth a two-day phone survey of all nine city leads before the board meeting, and that is the work Rohan assigned himself for the next thirty-six hours.

The nuances a learner must become aware of

Order of magnitude, not decimal precision

A Fermi estimate is trustworthy to roughly a factor of two or three, which for Rohan's number means "somewhere between five and fourteen thousand," not "9,016." Writing 9,016 on a slide without the range invites the room to argue about the last digit instead of the decision the number supports; the discipline is to state the range first and the point estimate only as its midpoint.

The decomposition is a choice, not a discovery

Rohan could have decomposed differently — by city rather than by trip, or by vehicle-age cohort rather than by fleet average — and would have arrived at a different but equally legitimate chain. There is no single correct decomposition; there is only a better or worse one, judged by whether each link can be anchored to something real and whether the links are close to independent of each other.

Anchoring beats guessing

The difference between Fermi estimation and simply making up a plausible number is the anchor: 4.2 trips per day came from a dashboard screenshot, not a hunch, and 1-in-3,000 came from three independent phone calls, not a single person's impression. An estimate with no anchor at any link is not a Fermi estimate; it is a guess wearing a Fermi estimate's clothes.

Independence is assumed, and it is often wrong

Multiplying the links together silently assumes they move independently of one another. In Ganana's case this is shaky: higher utilization likely correlates with higher breakdown probability, since a scooter ridden 4.2 times a day accumulates battery stress faster than one ridden 3.0 times a day. Treating the two as independent probably understates the true variance of the answer, which is a reason to keep the stated range generous rather than tight.

What it is routinely confused with

Fermi estimation is often conflated with market-sizing frameworks such as TAM/SAM/SOM, which use a similar multiplicative funnel but answer a different question — the addressable size of an opportunity rather than the magnitude of an operational quantity — and with statistical forecasting, which requires an actual dataset and produces a distribution, not a single anchored chain. Fermi estimation is the scaffolding used when neither a market study nor a dataset yet exists.

What it cannot tell you

Even a well-built estimate says nothing about when the breakdowns happen — whether they cluster in the monsoon weeks, or in the first ninety days of a scooter's life — nor about the mechanism behind them, nor about whether the predictive-maintenance sensors would actually prevent them rather than merely detect them sooner. A Fermi number answers "how many," never "why" or "what happens if we intervene."

The question a newcomer should always ask first

Before trusting any Fermi chain, ask which single link the final number is most sensitive to, and whether that link's range was itself anchored or guessed. If the widest-ranging link in the chain is also the one with the flimsiest anchor, the entire estimate inherits that flimsiness, however solid the other three links are.

Fermi estimation is a stopgap, not a permanent answer

The moment real data becomes available — in Ganana's case, ten days later when the warehouse migration finished — the estimate should be checked against it and either confirmed or replaced. Treating a Fermi number as a permanent metric, still cited in a deck a year later, is a misuse of the tool regardless of how carefully it was built.

How the idea changes by context

In a consumer product, Fermi chains typically decompose a single population's behavior — as Ganana did with its riders — and the anchors tend to come from internal usage data, however partial or stale. In a B2B setting the chain usually decomposes a smaller number of larger accounts: a logistics SaaS company such as Sankhya Freight, sizing how many trucks a prospective mid-size FMCG distributor operates before a sales call, might anchor on public information — the distributor's annual revenue divided by an industry-typical revenue-per-truck figure — because there is no internal usage data to draw on at all. In a marketplace, the chain must be built twice, once for each side: an artisan-goods marketplace such as Parimaan Bazaar estimating how many new sellers a rural-outreach push could bring on needs a separate anchored chain for addressable artisan clusters and for buyer demand in those regions, multiplied together only after each side is independently sized, since supply and demand rarely scale in lockstep.

The habit also differs by company stage. At an early-stage company with no dashboards at all, Fermi estimation is often the only tool available, and the discipline is to build the chain carefully the first time, since there is no ground truth to check it against for months. At a company Ganana's size, with real instrumentation that simply broke for ten days, the discipline is different: the estimate is explicitly provisional, and the team's job once the warehouse returns is to reconcile the Fermi number against the measured one and note the gap — a habit some product teams at larger firms, including a diagnostics company like Maapdand Health, formalize by logging every Fermi estimate that entered a decision and auditing it against real data once available, which over time calibrates who on the team tends to overestimate or underestimate which kinds of quantities.

Common mistakes

False precision. The symptom is a slide that states "9,016 breakdowns" with no range attached. The underlying misunderstanding is treating the multiplication of several guesses as equivalent to a measurement. The cheapest diagnostic: ask the presenter to rerun the chain with each input shifted twenty percent in either direction and watch how far the output moves; if it moves by thousands, the original precision was never real.

Resting the whole estimate on one anecdote. The symptom is that the entire chain traces back to a single person's recollection — one ops lead's "about two calls a day" — with nothing cross-checked. The misunderstanding is failing to identify, and then verify, the link the answer is most sensitive to. The cheapest diagnostic is simply calling two more people who would know and seeing whether their numbers land in the same neighborhood.

Skipping the absurdity bound. The symptom is an estimate that implies something impossible — for instance, a breakdown rate that would mean more scooters break down than complete trips — going unnoticed because nobody paused to sanity-check the chain against a known ceiling. The diagnostic is to compare the final answer against at least one independent known figure, such as total repair-ticket volume logged in the field-service system, even a stale one.

Treating the output as final. The symptom is a Fermi-derived number quietly becoming a permanent line in a recurring dashboard, cited months later as if it were measured. The misunderstanding is forgetting that the number was built to unblock one decision, not to stand indefinitely. The cheapest diagnostic is a literal label — "Fermi estimate, built 14 Sep 2026, supersede once warehouse data returns" — attached at the moment the number is created.

What good looks like

Two days later, Rohan walked into the board meeting with the decomposition chain drawn on a single slide, the range stated as 5,400 to 13,500 with a central case of nine thousand, and a note that a two-day survey of all nine city ops leads — completed the night before — had tightened the breakdown-rate band from 1-in-2,000–5,000 down to 1-in-2,600–3,400, moving the central estimate to roughly 8,600 with a narrower range of 7,000 to 10,600. He did not present the number as fact; he presented it as the best defensible estimate available given a ten-day data outage, showed exactly which assumption it depended on most, and showed the work he had already done to narrow that assumption. The board approved a ₹40 lakh phase-one pilot across two cities rather than the full ₹1.4 crore rollout, explicitly tied to replacing the Fermi estimate with measured breakdown data once the warehouse migration completed — precisely the staged, verifiable commitment a well-built estimate is supposed to earn.

Closing

Rohan's decision was not to trust the number blindly nor to wait ten days for certainty, but to size the investment to match the estimate's actual confidence: enough capital to test the idea, not enough to bet the year on a chain built in an afternoon. The reasoning he carried out of the room was that a defensible range, honestly labeled and tied to a plan for narrowing it, moves a decision forward faster than either a false-precise number or a stalled one. Having learned to build and defend this kind of chain under real time pressure, the next things worth his attention are market sizing through TAM/SAM/SOM, which chains several Fermi-style estimates together to size an entire opportunity rather than a single operational quantity, and the discipline of estimating feature impact, which uses the same multiplicative reasoning to forecast what a not-yet-built feature would actually change. Two questions worth sitting with afterward: in the last quick estimate you presented at work, which single input would you have bet real money was wrong — and did you say so out loud before someone else found it? And if you had exactly one phone call and one hour to spend narrowing your next estimate, which link in the chain would you spend it on?

Two questions to sit with.

2. If you had exactly one phone call and one hour to spend narrowing your next estimate, which link in the chain would you spend it on, and why that one rather than any other?

Fermi Estimation

Near-expert depth: how uncertainty actually propagates through a multiplicative chain, when decomposition is the wrong instrument, and what the field still argues about.

1. Two decisions, two weeks apart

On the afternoon of 3 February 2026, Meera Raghunathan, Head of Product at Nihai Speech AI in Bengaluru, was asked by her CEO to sign off on a pricing floor. Nihai builds voice agents that place loan-collection calls for non-banking finance companies, and was moving from per-seat licensing to per-minute pricing — a change sales wanted because it removed the seat-count negotiation, and the CFO wanted because it made revenue scale with usage. The floor would sit in twenty-four-month contracts. The complication was a feature not yet built: a second model running alongside the primary agent, scoring borrower sentiment and escalating distressed calls to a human. It would roughly double inference cost per minute, and nobody could say what that came to across a year, because no production traffic existed to measure. Nihai's gross margin on the voice product was 62%. A cost error of three times in either direction would take that to 80% or to negative.

Eight days later, on 11 February, Devesh Kamat, general manager of the connected-tools division at Hathoda Instruments in Pune, put a proposal to his board. Hathoda makes digital torque wrenches for vehicle assembly lines — the instruments that tighten a chassis bolt to a specified newton-metre and log the result. Devesh wanted to launch calibration-as-a-service: ₹18,000 per tool per year, under which Hathoda would take over the drift-checking and certification that plants now do in-house or through third-party labs. The service is brand-agnostic, so it would cover competitors' tools too. The build required ₹6 crore of mobile rigs and a fourteen-person field team. The number Devesh did not have was the one everything rested on: how many electronic torque tools in Indian assembly plants sit under a documented calibration regime at all. No industry body publishes it, ACMA's member surveys do not ask, and Hathoda's records covered only its own directly sold units.

Both are Fermi problems. They are not the same Fermi problem, and the difference is between a quantity decomposition can settle and one for which decomposition's real output is the discovery that it cannot.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Fermi estimation is the practice of producing a defensible order-of-magnitude answer to a quantitative question by decomposing the unknown into a short chain of factors, each anchored to something the estimator genuinely knows, and then recombining them — with the estimate's uncertainty tracked and reported rather than discarded. The precision claim is deliberately modest. Enrico Fermi's reputation rested on being reliably within a factor of two or three; his estimate of the Trinity yield in July 1945, made by dropping scraps of paper and pacing out how far the blast wave carried them, was in that band. The pedagogy that followed — Philip Morrison's Fermi problems, the Chicago piano tuners — taught that a quantity nobody has measured is not therefore unknowable.

The problem the method solves is scarcity of measurement, not of arithmetic. Its migration into business came through management-consulting case interviews from the 1970s onward, and later through a more serious literature: Douglas Hubbard's How to Measure Anything (2007), which reframed estimation as applied measurement, and Philip Tetlock's Superforecasting (2015), which argued the binding constraint was calibration rather than structure.

Four positions are held by serious people, and they disagree in ways that matter at the desk.

The decomposition school is Fermi's own, and the default taught in MBA programmes. It will sign: a chain of independently anchored factors beats one expert's holistic judgement, because independent errors partially cancel. It will not sign: more links are always better. The outside-view school — Kahneman and Lovallo, extended by Bent Flyvbjerg's megaproject work — holds nearly the opposite. It will sign: a base rate drawn from a comparable population of completed cases dominates any decomposition built from inside the project, resting on evidence that inside-view infrastructure planning overran by a median near 45% while reference-class forecasting narrowed the error. It will not sign: you can neutralise optimism bias by decomposing — decomposition, it argues, supplies more places for the same bias to enter while feeling more rigorous.

The calibration school declines to argue about structure. It will sign: the dominant error term is the human's overconfident interval, and calibration training measurably shrinks it. It will not sign: the point estimate is the deliverable — on this view an estimate without an interval is not a weak estimate, it is not an estimate. The measurement-minimalist position, Hubbard's sharpest contribution, will sign: a small sample almost always beats a careful estimate, and is cheaper than people assume; the Rule of Five holds that five random observations bracket the population median with 93.75% confidence. It will not sign that estimation substitutes for measurement, only that it is what you do in the hours before measurement is possible. A fifth, quieter position — the decision-theoretic sceptic — will sign: a number whose every plausible value leads to the same decision should not be computed at all, and will not sign the publishing of estimates as standing company metrics.

3. Mechanics: what experts do that the textbook leaves implicit

What separates a professional estimate from a classroom one is not the decomposition, which most competent practitioners do adequately, but the five operations around it.

Start from the threshold, not the quantity. The expert first asks what value would change the decision. Meera's threshold was arithmetic: at a contracted ₹4.10 per minute and a 55% gross-margin floor, total delivery cost could not exceed ₹1.85 per minute, of which the primary agent already consumed ₹1.10 — leaving ₹0.75 for the sentiment model and everything else. Devesh's was capital: the ₹6 crore build needed ₹3.2 crore of recurring revenue by year three to clear his division's hurdle, which at ₹18,000 per tool and a 25% attach rate meant an addressable pool near 7,100 tools. Both thresholds were fixed before either man estimated anything, which is what stops an estimate drifting toward the answer its author wants.

Estimate in log space. Experts do not write "about 180,000 calls, give or take". They write a 90% credible interval as a ratio: 90,000 to 360,000, a fourfold band. Multiplicative chains behave additively in logarithms. For a factor whose 90% interval runs from L to U, σ = ln(U/L) ÷ 3.29, a 90% interval spanning 3.29 standard deviations. The uncertainty of the product is then the square root of the sum of the squared σ values — errors add in quadrature, not linearly.

The consequence is the single most useful quantitative fact in this topic. Four independent factors each uncertain by a factor of two do not give an answer uncertain by a factor of sixteen. Each contributes σ = ln(2)/3.29 = 0.211; the total is √(4 × 0.211²) = 0.421; the product's 90% band is exp(2 × 1.645 × 0.421) ≈ 4.0. Uncertainty grows with the square root of the number of links, which is why decomposition is cheaper than intuition suggests — provided the links are genuinely independent.

Meera's chain, built on 4 February, ran: NBFC customers at end-FY27, times collection calls per customer per month, times handled minutes per call, times sentiment cost per minute, times twelve — medians multiplying to 42 × 180,000 × 2.4 × ₹0.42 × 12, about ₹9.14 crore a year.

Distinguish the median from the mean. Multiplying medians gives the median of the product, not its expected value. A product of independent lognormal factors is itself lognormal, its mean exceeding its median by exp(σ²/2) — at σ = 0.714, a factor of 1.29. Meera's expected annual cost was ₹11.8 crore against a median of ₹9.14 crore: a budget built from medians is underfunded by 29% here, and the gap widens sharply as chains get more uncertain. Practitioners who have never met this arithmetic underfund, then call the overrun bad luck.

Correct for correlation. Quadrature assumes independence; where two factors share a driver, variance picks up a cross-term of 2ρσ₁σ₂. Customer count and calls per customer are plausibly correlated at ρ ≈ 0.4, since a strong FY27 wins both more NBFCs and larger ones: that adds 2 × 0.4 × 0.211 × 0.421 = 0.071 to a variance of 0.509, pushing σ from 0.714 to 0.762 and the band from 10.5× to 12.2×. Modest here, ruinous when correlation is high and unnoticed.

Apply the split test before adding a link. Decomposing X into A × B improves matters only if A and B are known better, in relative terms, than X: formally, if σA² + σB² < σX². Devesh could estimate "tools per plant" directly at a threefold band (σ = 0.334, variance 0.111), or split it into "assembly stations per plant" times "tools per station" at twofold bands each (0.045 + 0.045 = 0.090). The split passes, narrowly. Had either child been a pure guess at a fourfold band, the split would have made the estimate worse while making the slide look more rigorous — the formal content behind the folk advice not to over-decompose.

4. When the method applies, stated as claims you can test

Four conditions can be checked before any arithmetic, and the honest answer is sometimes that the method does not apply.

Claim 1: every factor can be anchored to within roughly a factor of three. Devesh passes on all three links: plant counts from SIAM and ACMA directories, tools per plant from his field engineers' site visits, calibration-regime share from the fraction of plants holding IATF 16949 certification, which mandates measurement-system control. Meera fails on one. Inference cost per minute is not an unknown constant she lacks data on; it is a moving quantity, her providers having cut published per-token prices by roughly an order of magnitude in two years. A drifting factor is not badly measured, it is badly modelled.

Claim 2: the decision threshold sits at least two to three times from the central estimate. Devesh's threshold was 7,100 tools against a central estimate near 17,800 — a factor of 2.5, outside his band's lower reach, so the estimate decides the question. Meera's was ₹0.75 per minute against ₹0.42 — a factor of 1.8 on a link whose own band spanned 5.3×. Her estimate could not decide her question, and no further decomposition would change that. This is the estimate's most valuable output: it told her to stop estimating.

Claim 3: the links are approximately independent. Where they are not, the reported band understates risk and the correction above is the minimum response.

Claim 4: no cheap sample would beat the estimate. Meera's alternative cost ₹40,000 and a week: route 2,000 live calls through a shadow instance of the sentiment model and measure. Against a twenty-four-month pricing commitment, that is free. Where a sample is available, estimation is procrastination with arithmetic attached.

Beyond these, the method is actively misleading in three situations. When the distribution is heavy-tailed and the decision depends on the tail — fraud losses, outage costs, safety recalls — the mean is dominated by rare events no median-based chain represents. When the quantity is a sum of a few large items rather than a product of many small ones: enterprise revenue from six deals is a pipeline review, not a Fermi problem. And, most commonly, when the number will be laundered into a commitment — a range carried forward as a target has become something other than an estimate.

5. Hard edges

Multi-product firms hit the shared-denominator problem: two teams each build a chain starting from "active customers", and the sum double-counts every customer using both. The seam is organisational, not mathematical, and surfaces only when finance reconciles the two decks.

Two-sided markets hit a subtler version. Sandaasi Bazaar, a marketplace connecting small fabrication workshops to industrial buyers, sized a metros expansion by estimating addressable workshops and addressable buyer demand separately and multiplying the two through a match rate. Both chains contained a city factor, so the product implicitly squared the geography. The correct construction is one chain per city, summed — or to identify which side binds, in Sandaasi's case supply, since a buyer with no nearby workshop simply does not transact, and size that side alone.

Regulated products face a denominator defined by statute rather than judgement. Aujaar Health Systems, selling diagnostic-lab software, cannot estimate its addressable base from any internal chain, because the number governing procurement is the count of NABL-accredited laboratories — a published register with a legal definition. The expert move is to stop estimating and look it up, and to notice that a self-built chain would produce a number uncitable in a tender even if correct.

Hardware-plus-software adds a stock-versus-flow trap: an installed base is a stock, sales are a flow, and the bridge is a survival curve rather than a constant. Devesh's cross-check exploited exactly this, and it was the most persuasive thing he did.

AI-native products break a different assumption. Meera's cost link was non-stationary on a timescale shorter than her commitment: the estimate had a half-life. The expert treatment is to model the factor as a trajectory with a decay rate and integrate over the contract period — or, more honestly, to refuse the fixed commitment and negotiate a reset clause. A second loop is peculiar to AI products: better output raises usage, so cost and volume are coupled through quality and the correlation term is not small.

At the organisational seams, what mature companies say they do is keep an estimate register — every Fermi number logged with author, date, decision supported and supersede date. What most do is let the number escape into a deck, lose its range in the second retelling, and acquire the authority of a measurement by the fourth. The firms that genuinely run a register are the ones burned by a specific number they can still name.

6. Nine distinctions that separate the expert from the competent

Uncertainty grows as the square root of the chain length. The tell is a competent practitioner refusing to decompose "because the errors compound". They do compound — in quadrature. Four factor-of-two links give a factor-of-four answer, not sixteen. The obvious reading adds ranges rather than variances, and the consequence is that experts decompose more freely than colleagues, stopping for a different reason: not fear of compounding, but the split test.

Effort follows variance share, not factor size. The tell is a colleague refining the largest number in the chain. Variance share is quadratic in the log-band, so a link with a fivefold band carries roughly six times the burden of one with a twofold band, whether it reads 42 or 180,000. The obvious reading — the big number deserves the scrutiny — confuses magnitude with uncertainty.

The median of a product is not its mean. The tell is a budget built from multiplied medians that overruns most quarters without any single assumption being wrong. Multiplicative chains are right-skewed; the mean exceeds the median by exp(σ²/2) — 29% at σ = 0.7, 65% at σ = 1.0. Experts budget to the mean, plan to the median, and know which they are quoting.

Correlation is the silent variance. The tell is two links answering the same sentence — "if the year goes well". The obvious reading is that each link was estimated honestly, so the chain is honest. Shared drivers widen the true band well beyond the reported one: four links all driven by growth behave closer to one link with a very wide band.

The threshold precedes the estimate. The tell is that an expert's first question is "what would this number have to be for us to decide differently?" rather than "what is this number?" The obvious reading treats this as pedantry. It converts an unbounded estimation task into a bounded one, and frequently ends it, as it did for Meera.

An estimate that cannot clear its threshold has still succeeded. The tell is an expert reporting without embarrassment that the estimate is too uncertain to decide the question, and here is the measurement that would. The obvious reading is a failure to deliver. The opposite holds: producing a number precise enough to sound decisive and using it anyway is the failure that costs money.

Small samples dominate careful estimates. The tell is that the expert reaches for the phone or a log query rather than the spreadsheet. The Rule of Five startles most practitioners: five random observations bracket the population median with 93.75% confidence. The obvious reading — five is too few to say anything — is an intuition trained on significance testing, which answers a far more demanding question than "roughly where is the middle".

Ranges compress under social pressure. The tell is that the interval in the written pre-read is wider than the interval spoken in the meeting. People narrow intervals when asked to commit, in front of seniors, or after someone else has spoken a number first. Experts write intervals down before the discussion and treat in-meeting narrowing as a datum about the room, not the quantity.

Estimates have half-lives, and some are short. The tell is an expert attaching an expiry date to a number at the moment of creating it. The obvious reading is that a well-built estimate is durable. For any factor drifting faster than the decision horizon — inference prices, commodity costs, regulatory thresholds — durability is what it lacks, and a number reused after its inputs have moved is worse than none, because it carries unearned authority.

7. How it differs across product types and stages

In consumer products the law of large numbers works for you: the quantity is a large population times small, comparatively stable per-unit rates, so chains are reliable. In B2B the same arithmetic is often inappropriate, because the quantity is a sum over a few large accounts whose variance is dominated by whether three specific deals close. Enterprise adds a twist: the binding factor is usually time — procurement, security review, pilot-to-production conversion — so the sharpest chains put a duration where a naive chain puts a volume. In platforms and marketplaces the shared-geography trap above is the standard error, and the discipline is to size the binding side rather than both.

Hardware is where Fermi estimation is most reliable, worth saying plainly because it cuts against the assumption that physical businesses are harder. Physical quantities obey conservation laws and stock–flow identities; service lives, bill-of-materials costs and plant counts change slowly and cross-check from several directions, as Devesh showed. AI products are the mirror image: identical arithmetic, but unit cost and user behaviour move fast enough that the chain must be dated.

Across stages, what changes is what the estimate competes with. Pre-product-market-fit there is no measurement, so estimation is the only instrument and the discipline is honest intervals. At growth stage the decision is arbitrage: estimate, or spend a week of engineering measuring. At scale it becomes governance — the arithmetic is trivial, the difficulty is stopping fourteen teams carrying fourteen incompatible denominators into one budget review. Where there is no real difference, say so: the mathematics is identical everywhere. Only the quality of anchors and the cost of being wrong change.

8. Three worked cases, one of them a failure

Hathoda Instruments, February 2026 — the cross-check that carried the board. Chain A (Figure 3) gave 340 plants × 95 tools × 0.55 = 17,765 addressable tools. Chain B derived the same stock from flow: roughly 11,000 electronic torque tools sold into India annually times a seven-year mean service life gives an installed base near 77,000, of which his engineers put about 23% on assembly lines under a calibration regime — 17,710. The chains shared no input, so their agreement raised his confidence far more than either alone, and against a 7,100-tool threshold the decision cleared even at the pessimistic end. The board approved a ₹1.4 crore pilot across three OEM plants rather than the full ₹6 crore — a commitment sized to the estimate's confidence rather than its midpoint.

Randa Freight Exchange, 2024 — the chain that was six times wrong. Randa, a Hyderabad logistics marketplace, sized a GST e-invoicing add-on from roughly 1.4 crore registered GSTINs, of which 12% were assumed above the turnover threshold that mandates e-invoicing, 35% of those not already on a compliant ERP, and 4% convertible within eighteen months: about 23,500 accounts at ₹14,000 average contract value, or ₹32.9 crore. Eighteen months later the business had 3,900 accounts and ₹5.1 crore.

Two things killed it. The 12% was not an estimate but an unexamined placeholder with no anchor at any point in its life; thirty phone calls would have exposed it in an afternoon. And the two middle links were negatively correlated — firms above the turnover threshold were precisely those already running compliant ERPs — so the chain multiplied two numbers that could not both be high. The recovery was not analytical: of forty sales representatives hired against the forecast, twenty-six were redeployed to the core freight product over five months, fourteen let go, and ₹1.9 crore of committed spend written off. The product survives at a tenth of its planned scale and is profitable. The lasting change was procedural — every chain in a Randa business case must now name a source per link, and any link sourced to "assumption" must be sampled before the case is heard.

Nihai Speech AI, February 2026 — the estimate that ended itself. Meera's chain produced ₹9.14 crore against a threshold near ₹16 crore, but with a tenfold band and half the variance in one non-stationary factor. Her memo carried a single line: this estimate cannot distinguish a 72% margin from a 38% margin, so it cannot support a twenty-four-month floor. She then spent ₹40,000 shadow-routing 2,000 live calls through the sentiment model over six days, returning 2.1 handled minutes per call and ₹0.31 per minute — inside her band, but measured, with the band collapsed to roughly ±15%.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Four of the five are detectable in the first hour by someone who knows to look. The fifth, laundering, is detectable only by process, because by the time it is visible the number sits in someone else's deck. That asymmetry is why the register matters more than the arithmetic. Basula Grid Systems, an energy-metering firm that once built a three-year capacity plan on a demand estimate whose author had left the company, now stamps every estimate with author, date and supersede condition — and its analysts describe the stamp, not the method, as the change that mattered.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Decomposition versus the outside view. The decomposition case is that a chain makes every assumption inspectable, that independent errors partially cancel, and that in genuinely novel situations no reference class exists. The outside-view case at its strongest is Flyvbjerg's: across thousands of infrastructure projects, inside-view estimates were not merely noisy but consistently biased, and decomposition did not correct it while reference-class forecasting did. Both cannot be fully right about the same class of problem. Decomposition would be shown wrong if business estimates proved as systematically biased as megaproject budgets; the outside view would be shown wrong if the reference classes available to a product manager were too heterogeneous to yield usable base rates — the practical objection, since "SaaS products like ours" is not a reference class in Flyvbjerg's sense.

Ranges versus points. The calibration school insists the interval is the deliverable and that training reliably narrows overconfidence. The opposing position, held quietly by many operators, is that organisations collapse ranges to midpoints within two retellings, so a stated range buys nothing and costs credibility with boards that read hedging as weakness. It would be wrong if firms mandating intervals demonstrably made better capital decisions; its defenders note that nobody has shown this, and that the calibration studies measure forecast accuracy, not decision quality.

Estimating at all, versus building decisions that do not need the number. The sceptical position is that effort spent narrowing an estimate is better spent restructuring the commitment so the number stops mattering — staged investment, reset clauses, reversible pilots. Devesh's board took this route. Its defenders would sign that optionality dominates precision whenever the option is cheap, and would be wrong wherever it is not: long-lead capacity decisions, regulatory filings and pricing floors in signed contracts all force the number to be right first time.

Whether the skill transfers. A minority holds that Fermi performance is almost entirely domain knowledge — good estimators simply hold many anchors for that domain — and that the general technique, as taught in case interviews, selects for glibness. Its evidence is that estimation accuracy correlates poorly across domains. Opponents reply that the transferable part was never the anchors but the structure: threshold first, interval always, variance checked. The disagreement is unresolved and bears directly on how this topic should be taught.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied the method produces a tidy chain, a point estimate and a confident slide. Someone who has internalised it differs in four visible ways. They ask for the decision threshold before the data, and often stop there. They quote a band before a midpoint, and the band does not narrow when the room gets senior. They can say without discomfort which single assumption would have to be wrong for the conclusion to flip, having already spent an hour on that assumption and none on the others. And they abandon the method quickly: the strongest signal of expertise is a practitioner who builds a chain for twenty minutes, sees the answer turns on one link, and spends the day measuring that link rather than the week refining the chain.

12. What they decided

Meera Raghunathan did not endorse the pricing floor on 6 February. She endorsed it on 17 February, after the shadow run, at ₹4.10 per minute with a floor computed from a measured ₹0.31 rather than an estimated ₹0.42 — and with a reset clause at eighteen months, on the grounds that the input was drifting and no measurement could fix that. Her reasoning: the estimate had done its real job by telling her the estimate was insufficient.

Devesh Kamat took the pilot rather than the full build. His estimate cleared its threshold by a factor of 2.5 and was corroborated by an independent chain — enough to justify committing capital, not enough to commit all of it at once. His reasoning: the two chains agreed on the size of the pool but said nothing about the attach rate, the one factor his business case needed and no estimate could supply.

1. Meera's estimate and Devesh's estimate had comparable uncertainty bands. One was actionable and one was not. What exactly made the difference, and would you have been able to say so before building either chain?

2. Randa's fatal link — the 12% — was not disputed by anyone in the room. What does that suggest about where to spend scrutiny in a business case, and what would a review process that catches unanchored placeholders actually look like?

3. Devesh's two chains agreed within 0.3%. When would such agreement be evidence of nothing at all, and how would you tell the two cases apart?

13. Going deeper

Market sizing (TAM / SAM / SOM) applies this method to an opportunity rather than an operational quantity, inheriting every property discussed here — including the shared-denominator trap, where most TAM decks fail. Estimating feature impact points the same chain forward at something that does not yet exist, removing the option of measuring and raising the premium on honest intervals.

Reading a P&L supplies the anchors that make chains defensible; the best links on this page trace to a line item someone had already audited. Gross margin and cost to serve is the arithmetic behind Meera's threshold; contribution margin tells you whether an incremental minute is worth selling at all. Unit economics builds the whole business as one chain under the same variance rules. CAC, LTV and payback is the highest-stakes multiplicative estimate most product organisations make, and the one where correlation between links — churn and acquisition quality — is most routinely ignored. Cash flow, burn and runway is where median-versus-mean stops being academic: a runway computed from multiplied medians ends earlier than planned more often than not.

Market Sizing at Depth: What TAM, SAM and SOM Actually Measure

Sizing top-down and bottom-up is the easy part. The command comes from knowing how error compounds along an estimate, why two independent methods are usually not independent, and what happens when the unit of consumption itself starts moving.

1. Two rooms, two decisions, one arithmetic

On 9 March 2026, Ila Venkataraman spent the morning in a machine shop in Medchal, outside Hyderabad, looking at a tooling quotation she did not want to sign. Ila was Chief Product Officer of Paseri Cold Systems, which made battery-powered temperature loggers and the software that read them, sold to distributors legally obliged to prove that a vial of insulin had never crossed eight degrees between factory and chemist. The quotation was for injection-moulding tools and a second surface-mount line: ₹14.2 crore, seven months of lead time, and a capacity of 60,000 logger units a year once commissioned. Paseri had shipped 11,400 units in FY2026. Ila's board had asked the only question that mattered: was there a market that would absorb 60,000 units a year within three years, and how did anyone know?

Three weeks later and 570 kilometres south, Kabir Anand was answering a harder version of the same question in a Bengaluru meeting room with a term sheet on the table. Kabir had co-founded Nazhi AI, which drafted replies to GST and income-tax notices for chartered accountancy firms — the model read the notice, pulled the client's filings, and produced a submission-ready draft that a partner reviewed and signed. In January, Nazhi had moved from a per-seat subscription to a price per drafted notice. Since then, notices processed had risen 3.1 times and revenue per firm had fallen 19 per cent. The lead investor wanted a TAM. Kabir had three defensible numbers — one built on seats, one on notices, one on the hours of junior-associate labour the product displaced — and they ranged from ₹170 crore to ₹1,240 crore. He did not think any of the three was a lie.

Both decisions turn on the same craft, and neither is solved by picking a bigger number. Ila's is a capacity commitment against a physical market with a countable installed base. Kabir's is a valuation conversation about a market whose unit price is falling faster than most people in the room understand. What follows is why the standard treatment of TAM, SAM and SOM handles the first case tolerably and the second badly.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Market sizing is the estimation of the revenue or volume available to a firm in a defined market, over a defined period, by an explicit chain of assumptions. The conventional decomposition has three nested layers. TAM — total addressable market — is the annual spend that would exist if every entity with the underlying need bought a solution to it. SAM — serviceable addressable market — restricts TAM to what the firm's product, geography, channel and business model can reach. SOM — serviceable obtainable market — restricts SAM further to what the firm can plausibly capture within a stated horizon, given competitors, capacity and go-to-market throughput.

The vocabulary is younger than the practice. Corporate planning in the Ansoff tradition already decomposed a business into product-market cells; "total available market" entered technology sales planning in the 1970s and 1980s as a quota-setting device for allocating sales territories. The SAM/SOM refinement is largely a venture-capital artefact of the 1990s, invented to solve one pathology: founders asserting a large number with no visible derivation, and investors having no cheap way to interrogate it. The three layers are, in origin, an auditing device — they exist so a sceptical reader can locate the assumption they doubt. Much of what goes wrong with sizing comes from treating them as a forecasting device instead.

Four schools of practice disagree, and it is useful to know exactly what each will and will not sign.

The category school — strategy consulting, equity research, most industry analysts — holds that markets are real objects with measurable boundaries, and that the discipline lies in defining the category correctly and reasoning about share. It will sign: the total spend in an established category is knowable within a factor of two from published data, and a firm's share is constrained by structural facts about that category. It will not sign: a forty-account pilot tells you the shape of a national market.

The build-it school — the Fermi tradition, Steve Blank's customer-development lineage, most operating venture practice — holds that the only trustworthy number is one you can reconstruct from units you have personally observed. It will sign: a market size you cannot rebuild from countable units and measured prices is not evidence, whatever its provenance. It will not sign: the category aggregate should constrain your own bottom-up forecast.

The market-creation school — Christensen's nonconsumption argument and the jobs-to-be-done literature — holds that sizing an existing category measures the wrong quantity whenever the product serves people who currently buy nothing. It will sign: for a genuinely new category the relevant quantity is the population with the unmet job, times a willingness to pay that appears in no spend statistic. It will not sign: current category spend is a ceiling.

The instrumental school is a minority position held candidly by some investors: TAM is not an estimate but a narrative instrument for capital allocation, whose only legitimate function is to establish an order of magnitude. It will sign: precision beyond an order of magnitude changes no decision TAM is actually used for. It will not sign: a sizing model should be refined.

3. Mechanics in depth: the chain, and how error travels along it

Every sizing estimate, top-down or bottom-up, is a product of factors. Top-down starts from an aggregate and multiplies by narrowing fractions; bottom-up starts from a countable unit and multiplies by rates and prices. The structural difference that matters is not the direction of travel but the length of the chain and the quality of each link.

Consider Kabir's two chains. Top-down, from a report licensed from Marakkal Advisory: India's tax-and-compliance software spend, times the drafting-and-representation fraction, times the SMB fraction, times the software-versus-services fraction, times a capturable share — five links, every one a judgement. Bottom-up: CA firms in India, times the fraction handling enough notices to justify a tool, times notices per firm, times price per notice — four links, three measurable from Nazhi's own book of 610 customers.

Now the quantitative treatment, which is where competent practitioners stop and experts do not. When a quantity is a product of independent uncertain factors, the uncertainties combine multiplicatively. Writing each factor's uncertainty as a relative standard deviation σ the relative uncertainty of the product is approximately the root-sum-square:

σ_total ≈ √(σ₁² + σ₂² + … + σₖ²)

Kabir assigned honest σ values to his top-down links: ±35 per cent on the category aggregate, ±50 on the drafting share, ±40 on the SMB share, ±45 on the software-versus-services split, ±60 on capturable share. Root-sum-square gives √(0.1225+0.25+0.16+0.2025+0.36) ≈ 1.05, about ±105 per cent — an interval spanning roughly a factor of eight. His bottom-up chain, with ±12 per cent on firm counts, ±25 on the qualifying fraction, ±20 on notices per firm and ±10 on price, gives ≈ 0.36, a span of about a factor of two.

This is the real reason bottom-up is usually more trustworthy, and it is not the reason usually given. It is not that measurement beats inference in principle; it is that the bottom-up chain was shorter and its links tighter, and error in a multiplicative chain grows with both.

Two second-order effects follow. First, multiplying your central estimates does not give the expected value. If each factor is roughly lognormal the product is lognormal, and its mean exceeds its median by exp(σ²/2). At σ = 1.05 that factor is about 1.73: the number Kabir gets by multiplying best guesses sits near the median, while the probability-weighted average outcome is some 73 per cent higher.

Second, sensitivity and uncertainty are different things. In a pure product every factor has an elasticity of exactly one so ranking assumptions by impact is meaningless; what ranks them is how uncertain each is. The share of total variance contributed by factor i is σᵢ²/Σσⱼ². Figure 2 does this for Kabir's top-down chain,, and says what a sensitivity table hides: capturable share alone carries a third of the uncertainty, while refining the category aggregate — the link teams spend most time on, because a report exists for it — buys almost nothing.

The step usually left implicit is the last one: deciding what the estimate is for. Ila's number must survive a capacity commitment with a seven-month lead time, so she needs a lower bound she would bet tooling money on. Kabir's must survive eighteen months of being quoted back at him, so he needs a defensible interval and a named leading indicator.

4. When the framework applies, and when it misleads

Four conditions can be stated as testable claims. First: the category has a stable boundary — a competent outsider, given the definition, would count roughly the same entities in. Ila passes cleanly; a temperature-controlled pharmaceutical shipment is a regulated object with a CDSCO paper trail. Kabir fails partially; "AI drafting for tax practice" was not a category in 2024 and its boundary with general legal drafting is moving.

Second: the unit of consumption is stable over the horizon — what customers buy one of will still be what they buy one of in three years. Ila passes; a logger is a logger. Kabir fails outright, which is the central fact of his situation: his unit moved from a seat to a notice in a single quarter, and may move again to an outcome.

Third: price is exogenous to share — the firm can gain share without materially changing price. Ila roughly passes, though Chhatank Instruments' entry at a lower price has begun to bend it. Kabir fails; his price per notice is falling because model costs are falling and because Adhak Compliance Cloud is pricing against him.

Fourth: demand, not supply, is the binding constraint. Ila fails this one, and it turns out to be the most important thing about her decision, as Section 8 shows. Kabir passes, until inference capacity or auditor trust becomes a bottleneck.

Where is the framework actively misleading rather than merely weak? Three situations. When the product serves nonconsumption, TAM anchored on current spend understates it by construction, and the error is not random but systematically downward. When price is collapsing, a rupee-denominated TAM shrinks while the real opportunity grows, and a team that manages to the rupee number will under-invest exactly when it should press. And when the binding constraint is the firm's own throughput, SOM computed from demand is not merely imprecise, it answers a question nobody asked.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

Multi-product firms hit the additivity problem: TAMs computed per product cannot be summed, because the same customer budget appears in several of them. A distributor's compliance budget cannot simultaneously fund Paseri's loggers, its excursion-analytics module and its audit-reporting service at full price. Mature companies handle this by sizing the budget holder — total annual spend by this buyer on this problem — and allocating within it. Most say they do this; fewer actually do, because product lines are staffed against product TAMs.

Two-sided markets break nesting differently. There is a demand-side TAM and a supply-side TAM, and the realised market is a function of match rates, which are local. A national marketplace TAM is close to meaningless because liquidity does not travel: the honest construction is a sum over city-category cells, each with its own liquidity threshold, where cells below the threshold contribute zero rather than a little.

Regulated markets add a dimension most models omit: the addressable population is set by a rule that can change on a gazette notification. Paseri's SAM roughly doubled in 2023 when a revised schedule extended continuous-monitoring requirements to a wider class of biologicals. A sizing model with no policy term in it is a model that will be wrong on a date.

Hardware-plus-software is where units and rupees genuinely diverge. Ila sizes two markets that happen to share a customer: a durable-goods market with replacement cycles, and a subscription market with churn. The disciplined move is to size the installed-base trajectory in units first, then attach two revenue streams to it.

AI-native products are the least settled edge. When the marginal cost of an inference falls year over year, three quantities move at once: price per task falls, tasks per customer rise because work previously refused becomes economic, and the base widens into nonconsumption. Rupee TAM can shrink while unit TAM triples.

Finally, the organisational seam. Above a few hundred people, TAM is usually owned by strategy, SAM by marketing and SOM by sales, and the three use different definitions of "customer" — legal entity, buying centre and billing account. The nesting is then arithmetically false and nobody notices, because the numbers live on different slides. Dronmaan Systems, a large infrastructure-software firm, fixed this by making one team publish all three layers from a single customer master and forcing any disagreement into a written note.

6. Eight nuances that separate expert from competent

Chain length is the hidden variable. Practitioners argue about top-down versus bottom-up when the live variable is how many multiplications separate the evidence from the answer. The tell is a model with eleven rows where four would do: the obvious reading, that more detail means more rigour, is wrong: each added link adds variance unless it replaces a guess with a measurement.

Triangulation is usually circular. Syndicated market reports are frequently built from vendor guidance and interviews with the very vendors whose numbers are being checked. When a report and a vendor's own forecast agree, the agreement may carry no information at all. The tell is a methodology note citing "primary interviews with market participants"; the expert asks which participants, and who commissioned the study.

The unit of consumption drifts, and rupee TAM drifts with it. Seats become tasks, tasks become outcomes, and each shift re-denominates the market. The tell is a pricing page that changed while the sizing model did not. Unit TAM is the stable quantity; rupee TAM is unit TAM times a price that is itself a strategic variable.

Price is endogenous to share. The last increments of SOM are usually bought with discounts, so SOM in rupees is not SOM in units times today's list price. The tell is a model in which assumed share rises across the horizon while assumed realised price holds flat.

Deflation is not contraction. When price per unit of work falls faster than volume rises, revenue dips before it grows. The tell is revenue per customer falling while usage per customer climbs, which a revenue-only dashboard reads as deterioration. The obvious reading, that the market is shrinking, is wrong: it is being repriced downward into a larger population.

"Serviceable" means serviceable by your operations, not your product. Installers, implementation consultants, field technicians, regulatory filings and compute quota all cap throughput. The tell is a SOM that the firm could not physically fulfil if every prospect signed in the same quarter.

Substitution budgets convert at a discount. Counting displaced labour cost as available revenue overstates TAM badly, because organisations release headcount slowly and keep much of the saving. A defensible model carries an explicit conversion rate from displaced labour rupees to software rupees — typically well under a third — and states it. The tell is a TAM built on "the salary of the people this replaces" with no conversion term.

Sizing is reflexive. A large TAM on a slide licenses a hiring plan and a burn rate, which commits the firm to behaving as though the market were large — making a mis-sized market expensive rather than merely wrong. The tell is a headcount plan derived from TAM rather than from pipeline.

7. How it differs by product type and by stage

In consumer products, bottom-up begins from population and a penetration curve, and public data is usually good enough that top-down works as a genuine cross-check. In B2B and enterprise, bottom-up is normally stronger because the addressable set is enumerable — a named list of firms above a size threshold in a sector — and the chain is short: accounts times qualification rate times average contract value. That is Ila's situation, and it is the easiest case in the discipline. Platforms and marketplaces are the hardest, for the liquidity reason already given; the only honest construction is cell by cell with a threshold. Hardware forces an explicit unit model, a replacement cycle and a supply ceiling that software teams rarely face. AI products add the price-and-unit instability described above.

Stage changes which method deserves weight. India's pharmaceutical cold chain, by their count from CDSCO licensing data and distributor registries, ran on about 42,000 temperature-controlled vehicles and 9,400 cold rooms. Regulation required continuous monitoring on a growing subset of both. Paseri's realistic share of newly-monitored assets, against Chhatank Instruments and Kolaga Telemetry, was 22 per cent over three years.

Nazhi AI: deflation read correctly

Kabir's apparent problem was that revenue per firm had fallen 19 per cent. Decomposed: price per notice fell 31 per cent as inference costs dropped and Adhak Compliance Cloud priced aggressively, while notices per firm rose 3.1 times — but only among firms that had migrated, which was 42 per cent of the base. Blending migrated and unmigrated firms produced the 19 per cent decline. Within migrated firms it was up 2.1 times.

Kabir's revised presentation abandoned a single TAM figure. He sized unit demand — 12.2 million notices a year across the addressable firm base, — and modelled price per notice with explicit deflation and expansion assumptions, the latter covering the roughly 620,000 small businesses that answer notices today without professional help. The investor's question changed from "how big is the market" to "at what price does the SMB segment open", which was a question Nazhi could run an experiment on.

Khaandi Fresh: where the method failed

Khaandi Fresh, a business-to-business fruit-and-vegetable marketplace founded in 2021, sized its market top-down: India's wholesale fruit and vegetable throughput of roughly ₹6.5 lakh crore, times a 4 per cent take rate, gave a ₹26,000 crore TAM. Investors approved a fourteen-city expansion. By 2024 the company was running ₹9 crore a month of negative contribution and closed nine cities.

Three things had been wrong. Only about 18 per cent of throughput was gradeable and cold-chain-capable enough to transact on a marketplace at all, cutting the real base to ₹1.17 lakh crore. Realised take rate settled at 1.2 per cent, not 4, because commission compressed the moment a second platform appeared in a mandi. And liquidity was city-specific: below roughly 140 active buyers per category per city, match rates collapsed and the cell contributed nothing — yet the model had assumed every city contributed in proportion to its population. Corrected, the honest SAM was about ₹1,400 crore and Khaandi's three-year SOM perhaps ₹60 crore, against the ₹900 crore the expansion had been staffed for.

The recovery is instructive because it was not a smaller version of the same plan. Khaandi rebuilt the model city by city with an explicit liquidity threshold, kept the three cities above it, and repositioned from commission to working-capital financing and grading services, where the take rate held at 3.4 per cent because it attached to a service rather than to a match. The corrected arithmetic supported a ₹190 crore business — an order of magnitude below the original TAM, and a viable company. The failure was not optimism about share; it was summing cells that could not each clear their threshold.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

The commissioned aggregate. Early sign: the market report was licensed from a firm that also sells advisory work to vendors in the category. Diagnostic: who paid for this study, and whose guidance produced its base year? Cost late: a strategy anchored on a number the industry told itself.

Share assumed rather than earned. Early sign: a round share percentage — five, ten, fifteen — with no win-rate or pipeline evidence. Diagnostic: what is our observed win rate in contested deals, and what would have to change for it to double? Cost late: hiring built against a revenue plan the funnel never supported.

Summing sub-threshold cells. Early sign: a national figure produced by multiplying a city result by a population ratio. Diagnostic: what is the minimum viable density in a cell, and how many cells clear it? Cost late: Khaandi's nine cities.

Rupee myopia in a deflating market. Early sign: revenue per customer declining while usage rises, and a planning discussion framed as a revenue problem. Diagnostic: is unit demand growing faster than price is falling, and at what price does the next customer segment become addressable? Cost late: retreating from a market at the moment it opens.

Demand-side SOM in a supply-bound business. Early sign: a SOM that the delivery organisation could not fulfil if every prospect signed. Diagnostic: what is our monthly throughput ceiling, and what does it cost to move it? Cost late: capital committed at the wrong point in the chain — Ila's ₹14.2 crore, very nearly.

Point estimates masquerading as forecasts. Early sign: TAM quoted to three significant figures. Diagnostic: what interval would you accept a bet on? Cost late: commitments sized to a confidence nobody held.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether to size at all before product-market fit. The instrumental position, steelmanned: pre-fit, every input is unstable, the exercise consumes weeks of senior attention, and its output decides only whether to continue — a binary an order-of-magnitude guess answers as well. Its evidence is the observable fact that early-stage TAMs are almost never revisited after the round closes. For it to be wrong, sizing would have to change an operating decision — pricing, segment order, channel — and not merely a funding one. The build-it school says exactly that: building the model is what surfaces the qualification rate, which does change segment order.

Whether top-down data can ever be trusted. The category school's strongest form: for established categories with regulatory reporting — pharmaceutical logistics, insurance premiums, telecom revenue — official aggregates are audited, comparable across years, and far better than anything a startup could assemble. The build-it school's strongest form: the categories where top-down is good are precisely the ones where interesting opportunities are not, because well-measured markets are well-served markets. For the first to be wrong, published aggregates would have to be systematically biased rather than merely coarse; for the second, someone would have to show an unmeasured category that turned out to be well described by its nearest published aggregate. Neither side has decisive evidence, and honest practitioners route by situation rather than principle.

Whether to size the category or the job. For AI-native products this is live and unresolved. Sizing the category — tax software, in Kabir's case — produces a number anchored to what the incumbent technology could charge. Sizing the job — notices that must be answered, whoever answers them — produces a larger number that includes nonconsumption but rests on a willingness to pay with no market evidence behind it. What would settle it is evidence on how often price collapse recruits nonconsumers rather than merely transferring value to existing buyers, and that evidence is at present mostly anecdote.

Precision versus interval. A growing minority holds that sizing output should always be reported as a distribution with its variance decomposition shown. The objection is that boards demand a number and will pick one from the interval anyway, usually the top; the counter-argument is that stating the interval at least records who picked.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this produces a clean three-layer model with a defensible number at the bottom. Someone who has internalised it does four things differently. They ask what decision the number has to survive before they build anything, because a tooling commitment and a fundraising narrative need different estimates. They go straight for the loosest link rather than the most researchable one, and they can say which link carries a third of the variance. They keep units and rupees in separate columns, so that a price change is visible as a price change rather than as market movement. And they report a range with a named leading indicator attached — the one observable quantity that will tell them, within a quarter or two, which end of the range reality is heading for. Perhaps the clearest single marker: an expert is more interested in the disagreement between two estimates than in either estimate, because the gap localises the assumption nobody has tested.

12. What Ila and Kabir decided

Ila declined the ₹14.2 crore tooling commitment and bought incremental capacity of 18,000 units a year for ₹3.6 crore, arguing that a demand-derived forecast of roughly 11,900 loggers over three years did not justify 60,000 a year even at the optimistic end of her interval. She redirected ₹6 crore to commissioning teams, reasoning that if the mandate extended as her sales head expected, installation throughput — not moulding capacity — would bind. She named one indicator to track monthly: newly mandated assets appearing in tender documents.

Kabir presented no single TAM. He gave the investor a unit forecast with an explicit price path, an interval around each, and a decomposition showing that capturable share carried a third of the uncertainty in any top-down figure he could construct. He raised below what the ₹1,240 crore labour-displacement number would have supported and well above what the ₹170 crore notice-based figure alone would have justified — and kept the right to be believed eighteen months later.

Discussion questions

  1. Ila's demand and capacity estimates were nearly equal at the optimistic end of her interval. Which would you commit capital to first, and what would you need to observe within two quarters to reverse that choice?
  2. Kabir's three denominators differ by a factor of seven and none is dishonest. When is presenting all three an act of rigour, and when is it an evasion of the judgement you are paid to make?
  3. Where in your own market model is there an implicit threshold below which a segment contributes zero rather than a little — and have you ever written it down?

13. Going deeper

  • Fermi estimation — the parent technique. Matters next because chain discipline, not market knowledge, is what makes a size defensible.
  • Sizing an opportunity — adds cost, timing and strategic value. Unlocks whether a large market is worth entering at all.
  • Market entry strategy — converts a trusted SOM into a sequence of segments, cities and channels.
  • Reading a P&L — where a sizing assumption eventually lands, and where you watch a share assumption fail.
  • Gross margin and cost to serve — revenue available versus revenue worth having.
  • Contribution margin — tells you whether an incremental unit of SOM adds or destroys value; essential for capacity decisions like Ila's.
  • Unit economics — turns a bottom-up sizing model into an operating model, since both are built from the same unit.
  • CAC, LTV and payback — how much of SOM is capturable at a price that clears; the missing link between share and cash.
