Market Sizing: TAM, SAM, and SOM

How big is this really, and which sizing method should you trust — the analyst's report, or the number you built yourself from a pilot?

1. A number on a slide, a decision behind it

On the second Tuesday of October 2026, Rohan Kelkar stood in a Pune conference room rehearsing a single slide. Rohan was VP of Strategy at Painth Mobility, an EV-charging network that had spent three years wiring petrol pumps, office parks, and highway plazas across eight Indian metros. The company was raising a Series C, and the pitch depended on a new line of business: shared AC chargers installed inside gated housing societies, sold to resident welfare associations rather than to fleet operators. The board wanted one number before the term sheet was signed — how much annual recurring revenue could this business plausibly reach in three years — and Rohan had two candidate answers that disagreed with each other by a factor of four.

The first number came from a report Painth had licensed from Chowk Analytics, a Mumbai research house that had pegged India's residential EV-charging spend at several thousand crore rupees by FY2029 and implied Painth could capture a respectable slice of it. The second number came from Painth's own six-month pilot: forty housing societies wired for measurement, real metering data, real conversion rates, and an arithmetic build that Rohan had done society by society. The pilot number was much smaller than the report number. Rohan's problem was not that he lacked a market-sizing estimate — he had two of them — but that he had not yet decided which one deserved to anchor a fundraising conversation with investors who would hold him to it eighteen months later.

2. The idea

Market sizing is the practice of estimating, with a stated method and named assumptions, how much revenue or volume is available to a company in a given market — broken into three nested layers. TAM (Total Addressable Market) is the revenue that would exist if every possible customer for this category of need, anywhere the company could conceivably operate, spent money on it. SAM (Serviceable Addressable Market) narrows that to the slice the company's actual product, geography, and business model can reach — not everyone who could theoretically want the thing, but everyone the company could realistically sell to. SOM (Serviceable Obtainable Market) narrows further still, to the revenue the company can plausibly capture within a specific time horizon given competition, capacity, and go-to-market reality.

The three-letter framework does not have a single named inventor; it crystallised out of strategic-planning and venture-capital practice through the 1980s and 1990s as a shorthand for a much older idea in corporate planning — that a market must be decomposed before it can be forecast, because "the market" is not one number but a funnel of narrowing assumptions. What TAM/SAM/SOM solved was a specific failure mode: founders and executives asserting market size as a single confident figure, usually large, with no visible path from evidence to conclusion. The sentence Rohan could repeat in the boardroom without sounding glib was this: a market size is only as trustworthy as the chain of assumptions that produced it, and the chain matters more than the number at the end of it.

3. How it actually works

Sizing runs in two directions, and a rigorous exercise uses both, not one. The top-down approach starts from an authoritative aggregate — an industry report, a government statistic, a total addressable population — and successively multiplies it by narrowing fractions: this slice is residential rather than commercial, this slice is in metros Painth already serves, this slice is winnable given competitors. Each multiplication is a judgement call, and top-down sizing is only as good as the fractions applied at each step, which are frequently guessed rather than measured.

The bottom-up approach starts instead from a unit of demand the company can actually observe or estimate directly — a customer, a transaction, a physical location — and builds upward: how many such units exist, what fraction are truly ready to buy, what revenue does a converted unit generate, and therefore what is the achievable total. This is the same discipline as Fermi estimation, the technique of decomposing an unknown quantity into a chain of smaller, more estimable quantities with explicit assumptions at each link — sizing is that technique applied specifically to markets, where the "unit" is a customer, an account, or a transaction rather than an arbitrary physical quantity.

The step practitioners usually skip is writing the assumptions down as a visible list, with a source or a confidence level attached to each one, so that anyone downstream — a board member, an investor, a colleague six months later — can see exactly where the number would break if reality diverged from the assumption. A bottom-up model built from forty pilot societies is not more "true" than a top-down number from a paid report; it is more inspectable, because every input traces to something the team actually measured.

4. A worked example, line by line

Rohan's top-down SOM was built the way most board slides are built. Chowk Analytics sized India's total EV-charging spend at ₹16,000 crore by FY2029. Residential and society-based charging, per the same report, was 35% of that total — ₹5,600 crore — which became Painth's SAM. Rohan then assumed Painth could capture 6% of that SAM within three years, a figure chosen because it sat between the shares held by two more established rivals, Sarafa Charge and Melaa Urja, in categories the report tracked. Six percent of ₹5,600 crore is ₹336 crore. That was the number on the original slide.

The bottom-up number came from the pilot itself. Painth's GIS database, cross-checked against municipal RWA (resident welfare association) registries, showed roughly 40,000 gated housing societies with 100 or more units across the eight metros where Painth already had charging depots — this was the addressable count, a figure the company had actually verified rather than licensed. The pilot's central finding was a threshold effect: a society's managing committee would approve shared charging infrastructure only once at least three resident households already owned an EV, because that was the point at which enough residents lobbied for it to overcome the committee's institutional caution. In the forty pilot societies, five crossed that threshold within six months — 12.5%, rounded to 12% for the model. Applied to the full base, that is 4,800 qualifying societies today.

5. The nuances a learner must sit with

Nesting only holds if the definitions match

TAM, SAM, and SOM are only truly nested — each one strictly inside the last — if every layer uses the same units, the same time period, and the same notion of "market." A common and quiet error is to define TAM as annual spend and SOM as lifetime customer value, or to define TAM by units sold and SAM by revenue; the circles in Figure 1 stop meaning anything the moment the definitions drift between layers.

Triangulate; do not choose

The instinct when two methods disagree is to pick the one that supports the story already being told. The more disciplined move is to treat the gap itself as the finding — a ₹336 crore top-down figure against an ₹81–134 crore bottom-up figure is not a contradiction to resolve by selecting a side; it is evidence that the report's assumed 6% share is not grounded in anything Painth has actually observed, and should be replaced or discarded.

Need is not the same as current spend

A market defined by what people currently pay for understates a genuinely new category, because spend has not yet caught up to latent need — few housing societies were budgeting for EV chargers in 2023 because almost no one needed one yet. A market defined by underlying need, in contrast, can overstate a mature category by counting people who will never convert. Rohan's team had to be explicit about which definition Chowk Analytics' report actually used, and it was not obvious from the report alone.

SOM is a function of time, not a fixed ceiling

"SOM" without a stated horizon is close to meaningless — three-year SOM and one-year SOM are different numbers built on different capture curves, and presenting one without saying which invites the listener to assume whichever is larger.

Small pilots carry wide error bars

Five out of forty societies crossing the threshold is a real signal, but it is also a small sample: the true rate could plausibly be anywhere from 8% to 18% with reasonable confidence, and a model that reports "12%" without acknowledging that range is quietly more precise-sounding than the underlying data supports.

Regulatory and physical constraints narrow SAM before competition does

Not every society with three EV owners can actually host a shared charger — transformer capacity, parking-lot ownership disputes, and state electricity-board approval processes all remove candidates before Painth's sales team ever gets involved. These constraints belong in SAM, and folding them into SOM instead (as "competitive loss") understates how structurally limited the market already is.

What sizing cannot tell you

A rigorous SOM tells you how much revenue is plausibly available; it says nothing about whether Painth can defend that revenue once Sarafa Charge or Melaa Urja respond, whether the unit economics of installing and servicing a charger actually turn a profit at that volume, or whether the company has the operating capacity to wire 4,800 societies without its installation quality collapsing. Sizing answers "how big," never "can we actually win it and make money doing so."

Sizing an opportunity is a broader exercise than sizing a market

TAM/SAM/SOM measures the ceiling on demand; "sizing an opportunity," the topic this one unlocks, adds the cost side, the timing, and the strategic value of entering now versus later — a market can be large and the opportunity small if the cost of capturing it exceeds what the revenue justifies.

6. How the picture changes by product type and by stage

In consumer products, bottom-up sizing typically starts from population and a penetration curve — how many people in the target demographic, what fraction plausibly adopt in a given year — and top-down numbers from industry reports tend to be more reliable as sanity checks because large, liquid consumer categories are well tracked by public data. In B2B and enterprise products, bottom-up is usually the more trustworthy default because a sales-led company can often enumerate its actual addressable accounts — a named list of companies of a certain size in a certain sector — and multiply by an observed average contract value, which is a far shorter inferential chain than a market-research aggregate. Marketplace products complicate both approaches because liquidity is local: a national TAM is meaningless if supply and demand cannot find each other within a given city or category, so a marketplace's credible SAM is usually built city by city and only summed afterward, never estimated as one national percentage.

Stage matters as much as product type. For an early-stage company like Painth's new housing-society line, bottom-up is close to the only credible method, because there is no track record to project from and a licensed report is, at that stage, closer to marketing collateral than to evidence — Painth's pilot data was worth more than Chowk Analytics' report precisely because Painth could trace every number in it. For a large, established company entering an adjacent category, top-down becomes more useful, because the company's own market-share data and its competitors' disclosed figures give the top-down fractions real grounding rather than guesswork — the same method that was weak for a forty-society pilot becomes strong once a company has three years of category-wide data behind it.

7. Common mistakes

The decorative TAM slide. The symptom is a large, round market-size number presented with confidence and no visible derivation. The underlying error is treating TAM as a motivational device rather than a diagnostic one. The cheapest test: ask the presenter to walk the number back to its source formula in sixty seconds: if they cannot, the number was chosen for its size, not its accuracy.

SOM without a horizon. The symptom is a SOM figure quoted as if it were permanent. The underlying error is conflating "obtainable" with "obtainable eventually," collapsing SOM back into TAM. The diagnostic is a single follow-up question: SOM by when?

Linear scaling of a pilot across dissimilar geography. The symptom is a national rollout projection built by multiplying the pilot's conversion rate by the national population share. The underlying error is assuming the conditions that produced the pilot's conversion rate — Pune and Bengaluru's relatively mature RWA governance, for instance — hold everywhere. The diagnostic is asking what specifically differs about transformer capacity, committee structure, or EV adoption in the cities being added, and whether the pilot rate would still hold there.

Stacking unrelated revenue lines into one TAM. The symptom is a TAM built by adding categories that the product could not plausibly serve with a single offering — charging revenue, EV financing revenue, and insurance revenue summed into one figure. The underlying error is measuring the size of an industry rather than the size of the specific thing being sold. The diagnostic is checking, line by line, whether the current product could realistically capture each included revenue stream without becoming a different company.

8. What good looks like

Two weeks after the disagreement surfaced, Rohan brought both numbers to the board rather than picking one. He presented the top-down ₹336 crore SAM-derived figure explicitly labelled as an upper bound drawn from Chowk Analytics' assumed 6% share, then walked through the bottom-up build society by society, ending with a range — ₹81 crore at the pilot's observed threshold-crossing rate, ₹134 crore if that rate accelerated as the team believed it would. He named the single assumption the range hinged on, said plainly that the sample behind it was forty societies, and proposed that Painth raise enough to fund a staged three-city rollout rather than the original eight-city plan, with the threshold-crossing rate tracked monthly as the metric that would tell the board, in real time, which end of the range the business was actually landing on. The board approved the smaller, better-evidenced ask. Nobody in the room mistook the ₹336 crore figure for a promise.

9. What Rohan decided, and what to learn next

Rohan anchored the Series C pitch on the bottom-up range, not the top-down report figure, and he kept the report's number in the deck only as context for the size of the category Painth was entering, not as a claim about what Painth itself would capture. The three-city staged rollout was smaller and less exciting than the original eight-city plan, but it was a number Rohan could defend line by line in front of an investor a year later, which the ₹336 crore figure was not. The next topic worth studying is sizing an opportunity — because a defensible SOM answers how much revenue is available, not whether capturing it is worth what it costs — followed by market entry strategy, which asks how and in what sequence to actually go after the SOM once it is trusted.

Two questions to sit with:

1. The next time you see a market-size number in a deck, can you reconstruct, in your head, the chain of multiplications that produced it — and which single link in that chain, if wrong, would break the whole figure?

2. When your own top-down and bottom-up estimates disagree by several multiples, what would it take for you to trust the smaller, harder-won number over the larger, easier one — and would you actually present the smaller number to a room that wanted the bigger one?

Fundraising and Investor Expectations

What a board needs the product story to prove at each stage — and why two competent teams, looking at the same numbers, reach opposite conclusions about what to show.

Section OneOpening: Two Rooms, Eleven Days Apart

On 4 March 2025, in a converted warehouse in Bermondsey, Priya Raman, VP Product at Latchkey, laid three printouts on the table in front of her CEO. Latchkey sold a self-service scheduling tool to independent physiotherapy clinics: £49 per clinic per month, 4,100 paying clinics, £2.4m ARR growing 78% year over year. Logo churn ran at 2.4% monthly. The company had £3.1m in the bank and was burning £310k a month — ten months of runway, and the CFO wanted a term sheet signed by July.

The three printouts were three different stories. The first showed the top-line curve and nothing else: a clean hockey stick. The second showed net revenue retention, which was 91% — below water, because clinics were single-seat and there was nothing to expand into. The third showed a cohort chart for a new multi-site product, six weeks old, 38 accounts, average contract value £680 a month, and zero churn because nobody had had time to leave. Priya's argument was that the third printout was the only honest Series A story, and also the one with the least evidence behind it.

Eleven days later, on 15 March, Marcus Adeyemi sat in a Boston conference room with the two outside directors of Verity Loop, a Series B company selling an AI-native contract review system to insurance carriers. Verity Loop had $9.2m in ARR from nine customers. Gross margin was 54% — inference costs on long documents were brutal — and two of the nine contracts, worth $3.4m together, renewed in Q4. The company had eighteen months of runway and no immediate need to raise. The question on the table was whether to spend $4m of the next twelve months buying gross margin (model distillation, caching, a smaller fine-tuned model) or buying logos (two more carriers, a compliance certification, a partner channel).

Marcus's instinct was margin. His lead investor's instinct was logos. Both were arguing about the same underlying thing: what the Series C buyer would need to believe, and which proof took longer to manufacture.

These two decisions sit at opposite ends of the same discipline. Priya is choosing which claim to make. Marcus is choosing which claim to make true. In both cases the binding constraint is not the quality of the product but the arithmetic of runway — the reason fundraising exists at all.

Section TwoThe Idea, and the Schools That Disagree About It

A precise definition: fundraising is the exchange of ownership for time, and investor expectations are the set of beliefs a buyer of that ownership must hold in order to find the price rational. A product story is the mechanism by which those beliefs are formed, and it is judged not by whether it is interesting but by whether it retires a specific risk that the stage in question exists to retire.

The intellectual lineage runs through three sources. The first is options theory: Steven Kaplan and Per Strömberg's work on venture contracts in the early 2000s framed staged financing as sequential real options — an investor buys the right, not the obligation, to fund the next tranche, and the price of that right falls as uncertainty falls. The second is Steve Blank and Eric Ries's customer-development tradition, which reframed a startup as a search for a repeatable model and, crucially, named the milestones: problem/solution fit, product/market fit, then scale. The third, more recent and more quantitative, is the SaaS-metrics canon — David Skok, Bessemer's cloud indices, the OpenView and ICONIQ benchmark reports — which gave boards a shared vocabulary of NRR, magic number, payback and Rule of 40.

Three schools disagree, and it matters which one is sitting across the table.

The narrative school — most visible in the writing of early-stage generalists and in the practice of seed funds that write many small cheques — holds that at the earliest stages metrics are noise, that the only real question is whether a large market is being entered by people with an insight others lack, and that over-instrumenting a seed story signals small ambition. The metrics school holds that founders systematically deceive themselves, that narrative is precisely what cannot be audited, and that the honest move is to identify the two or three numbers that would be true if the thesis were true and show them, warts included. The third, less often named, is the portfolio-construction school: the argument that investor expectations are not really about your company at all but about fund mathematics. A fund that must return 3x on $400m needs several outcomes above $3bn; therefore it will reject a company with excellent economics and a $600m ceiling, not because the story is weak but because it cannot move the fund.

The disagreement is sharpest on one question: does early traction predict anything? The metrics camp points to the reasonably strong empirical relationship between month-6 retention curves and eventual outcomes. The narrative camp points out, correctly, that the survivorship bias in that data is enormous, and that several of the largest outcomes of the last two decades showed uninspiring metrics at Series A because the product was mid-transformation.

Section ThreeMechanics: What Experts Actually Do

The operative craft is not deck design. It is working backwards from the next round to the milestone set that makes it raisable, then working backwards again to the capital and time required to hit that milestone with margin for error.

The arithmetic runs like this. Suppose Latchkey raises £8m. The Series B buyer, eighteen to twenty-four months out, will want roughly £8–10m ARR with NRR above 105% and CAC payback under eighteen months. That means Latchkey must more than quadruple revenue and invert its retention profile. Priya's job is to notice that those are two separate proofs, that the second is a product problem and not a sales problem, and that the second cannot be started after the round closes because the evidence needs twelve months of cohort data to be legible. This is the single most under-taught mechanic in the discipline: the proof you will need at the next round must be instrumented one round early, because cohort evidence has a manufacturing lead time that money cannot shorten.

Second-order effects that are usually left implicit. First, the round you raise sets the bar you must clear: a higher valuation is not free, it is a promise to produce a larger next-round proof, and the graveyard of 2021-vintage companies is full of teams who priced themselves out of their own next milestone. Second, dilution is a product decision — choosing a longer, more capital-intensive proof means giving away more of the company, which is why a PM's packaging experiment that shortens payback by four months is economically equivalent to several points of equity. Third, investors underwrite the rate of learning, not the level of performance; the most persuasive board material is usually a sequence showing that a hypothesis was named, tested, and either killed or scaled, because that is the only observable proxy for how the team will behave with the new money.

The diagnostics experts actually reach for are few. Magic number (net new ARR in a quarter divided by prior-quarter sales and marketing spend) tests whether spend converts. Cohort retention by signup month, plotted as a surface, tests whether the product is getting better or the market is getting shallower. Burn multiple (net burn divided by net new ARR) is the single most compressive number in the discipline — it collapses growth, efficiency and margin into one figure and is nearly impossible to dress up. And gross margin by cohort, which in AI-native companies is now the number that most often kills a round.

Section FourConditions: When the Frame Applies, and When It Does Not

The stage-gate framework rests on three testable claims. Claim one: the business has a repeatable unit that can be counted and whose behaviour over time is informative. Claim two: the capital required is large relative to what revenue can fund, so ownership must be exchanged for time. Claim three: the outcome distribution is wide enough that a venture fund's mathematics work.

Latchkey satisfies all three, but only just. Its unit — a clinic — is countable and its cohorts are legible. But its £49 price point implies a market ceiling that a large fund will test hard, which is why Priya's multi-site product is not a distraction from the fundraise but the substance of it: it is the only available answer to the portfolio-construction objection. If Latchkey cannot show a path from £49 to £680 per account, the honest conclusion is that it is a good business and a poor venture asset, and the correct instrument is debt or a growth-equity buyer, not a Series A.

Verity Loop fails claim one in an interesting way. With nine customers, there is no cohort. Nine data points cannot generate a retention curve; they generate anecdotes. This is the enterprise exception, and it changes the entire evidence regime: instead of statistical proof, investors accept depth proof — usage telemetry inside accounts, seat expansion, signed expansions, and named-executive sponsorship that survives a sponsor's departure. Marcus's real Series C risk is not margin or logos in the abstract; it is that two contracts represent 37% of revenue and renew in the same quarter as any plausible raise.

Section FiveHard Edge Cases and the Seams

Multi-product companies hit the attribution seam. A board sees consolidated ARR growth of 60% and is satisfied; a sophisticated investor decomposes it and finds product one growing 12% while product two, at a tenth the size, grows 400%. The correct expectation is that the board is underwriting the second S-curve, and the diagnostic is whether cross-sell into the installed base outperforms cold acquisition. If it does not, the company has two businesses sharing an office, not a platform.

Two-sided marketplaces hit the liquidity seam. GMV is the number most easily inflated and least informative. Experts ignore it in favour of match rate by geography and cohort, repeat rate on the constrained side, and take rate durability. The hard edge is that marketplaces look terrible on blended metrics while they are geographically expanding — a healthy marketplace entering ten new cities shows deteriorating aggregate liquidity. Mature operators solve this by presenting a single mature market as the "proof city" and the rest as investment, an approach that is honest when the proof city is genuinely representative and a fraud when it is the founder's home town with unrepeatable supply.

Regulated products hit the gate seam: value accrues in step functions at approval, so the linear-progress narrative is unavailable and investors instead underwrite regulatory probability and cash-to-gate. Hardware-plus-software hits the margin-mix seam: hardware gross margin of 22% and software of 85% blend into a number that means nothing; the real question is attach rate and whether hardware is a customer-acquisition cost dressed as revenue. Mature practitioners in this category report hardware separately and defend it as a distribution channel with a measurable payback.

AI-native products — Verity Loop's world — hit two seams at once. The first is cost-of-goods drift: unlike SaaS, marginal cost rises with usage, so the healthiest customers can be the least profitable, and gross margin must be shown by cohort with a credible curve toward 70%+. The second is the durability question: investors now routinely ask what survives the next foundation-model release. The consensus answer, insofar as one exists, is that defensibility lives in proprietary workflow data, integration depth and regulatory posture, not in model quality. But this is exactly where the market is least settled.

Section SixNuances That Separate Expert from Competent

1. The round is priced on the story you will tell next, not this one. Competent teams optimise the current raise; experts model the M18 board slide first and reverse-engineer today's roadmap from it. The tell-tale sign of expertise is a PM who can name, unprompted, the specific chart that must exist in fifteen months and the instrumentation shipped this quarter to create it.

2. Valuation is a liability with a coupon paid in milestones. Raising at 40x forward ARR obliges the company to grow into the multiple or face a down round, which damages hiring and customer confidence more than it damages the cap table. Experts routinely take a lower headline price for a cleaner structure, and the recognisable sign is a founder who asks about liquidation preference and participation before asking about valuation.

3. Structure is where the real negotiation happens. A 1x non-participating preference at $100m post is a different company from a 2x participating preference at $140m post; the second looks better in the press release and is worse for everyone below the preference stack. The tell: a team that models the founder-and-employee payout at three exit values, not one.

4. Net revenue retention is a product architecture decision made years earlier. Latchkey's 91% NRR is not a customer-success failure; it is the consequence of selling a single-seat tool to a single-site buyer. Experts recognise that expansion revenue must be designed into the pricing metric — per-site, per-claim, per-GB — long before the board asks about it. The tell is a PM who talks about the value metric rather than the price.

5. Burn multiple is the hardest number to lie about. Net burn over net new ARR: under 1.5 is excellent, over 3 is a warning, over 5 at Series B is usually terminal. Experts quote it unprompted because it pre-empts the question; the absence of it from a deck is itself diagnostic.

6. The concentration question is asked late and kills deals. Verity Loop's two-contract exposure is the sort of thing that surfaces in week five of diligence and repriced the round. Experts surface it in week one with a mitigation plan, because disclosed risk is discounted and discovered risk is penalised.

7. There is a difference between a metric that is bad and a metric that is not yet meaningful. Thirty-eight accounts with zero churn prove nothing. Experts say so explicitly and offer a leading indicator instead — weekly active sites, depth of configuration, a signed expansion — rather than presenting a statistic they know to be immature. The tell-tale sign is a presenter who states the sample size before the result.

8. Fund mathematics is a constraint on your story, not a judgement of your business. A rejection framed as "not venture scale" is information about the fund, and experts respond by changing the investor, the instrument, or the ambition — not by inflating the TAM slide, which is the single most easily detected form of dishonesty in the category.

9. The best evidence is a killed hypothesis. Boards trust teams that show a test that failed and the resource reallocated within the quarter. The tell: a board deck with a section titled "what we stopped."

10. Runway is measured to a milestone, not to zero. A company with nine months of cash and a proof that matures in eleven should raise a bridge or cut burn today. Experts run this comparison monthly; competent practitioners run it when the CFO raises it.

Section SevenHow It Differs by Product Type and Stage

ConsumerUnprompted retention curves flattening above zero; organic share of acquisitionPaid growth masking a leaky bucket; D30 that never plateaus

Stage changes the burden of proof more than type does. At seed, a team is underwritten on insight and a retention signal from a small population. At Series A, the question becomes repeatability: can the motion be described as a machine with inputs and outputs? At Series B, efficiency: does incremental spend produce proportionate revenue? At Series C and beyond, durability: is there a P&L in here, with a credible path to free cash flow and a Rule of 40 above the median. The 2021-to-2023 repricing did not change this ladder; it raised every rung and moved the emphasis from growth rate to burn multiple.

Section EightWorked Examples

Latchkey, reframed

At £2.4m ARR, 78% growth, £310k monthly burn: net new ARR over the last twelve months was roughly £1.05m; net burn was £3.7m. Burn multiple: 3.5 — poor. CAC was £420 with monthly gross profit of £38 per clinic, giving payback of 11 months, which is fine, meaning the burn multiple problem is not acquisition efficiency but churn: at 2.4% monthly logo churn, the company loses about £58k of ARR each month and refills the hole before it grows. NRR of 91% means every £1m of new sales produces only about £0.78m of durable revenue after a year.

The multi-site product changes the arithmetic. At £680 ACV against £49, thirty-eight accounts represent £310k of annualised revenue — 13% of the company, built in six weeks. If those accounts churn at 0.8% and expand, NRR moves above 105% within four quarters. Priya's proposal: raise a smaller £5m round at a lower valuation, present the multi-site cohort as an explicit early signal with the sample size stated, and commit to an M15 board proof of NRR above 105% on a cohort of 200+ multi-site accounts.

Verity Loop, and the failure

Verity Loop's predecessor case is instructive. In 2023 a comparable company — call it the cautionary comparator — raised a $60m Series B at $340m post on $7m ARR, 85% growth and gross margin reported as 71%. The 71% was blended across a legacy rules-based product at 88% and the AI product at 41%. In diligence for the Series C, eleven months later, the buyer decomposed the margin, found the AI cohort's margin had fallen to 34% as usage grew, and withdrew. The company had seven months of cash, cut 40% of headcount, and raised a structured inside round at a 55% discount with a 2x participating preference that wiped out common.

The recovery took nineteen months and was entirely a product exercise: a routing layer that sent 70% of documents to a distilled model at a twentieth of the cost, aggressive caching of clause-level embeddings, and a repricing from per-seat to per-document with a volume floor that protected margin on heavy users. Gross margin on the AI cohort reached 68%. The company raised a clean round at roughly the original Series B valuation — three years late, with the founders holding half of what they had. The lesson Marcus drew, and the reason he favours margin over logos: a margin problem compounds silently and is discovered by someone else at the worst possible moment.

Section NineFailure Modes and the Diagnostics That Catch Them

The recurring failures are few and predictable. Raising into an unproven milestone — taking money at a price that requires a proof nobody has started. Diagnostic: "What chart must exist at the next raise, and is it instrumented today?" Blended-metric concealment, usually unintentional. Diagnostic: "Show me this number split by product, cohort and segment — and show me the worst slice." Growth purchased at a deteriorating burn multiple. Diagnostic: "What is net burn divided by net new ARR, this quarter and last?" Expansion designed in after the fact. Diagnostic: "What is the value metric, and what does a customer buy more of as they succeed?" Concentration discovered in diligence. Diagnostic: "What percentage of ARR renews in the same quarter as the raise closes?" Runway measured to zero rather than to milestone. Diagnostic: "How many months between evidence maturity and cash-out?" And finally the TAM inflation reflex, which experienced investors treat as a character signal rather than an analytical error.

Section TenWhere Experts Genuinely Disagree

On whether to optimise for the metric or the machine. One camp holds that a company should identify the two or three numbers the next buyer will underwrite and manage explicitly to them, because capital is the binding constraint and failure to raise ends everything. The evidence: a long list of excellent products that died with good retention and a bad burn multiple. The counter-camp holds that managing to investor metrics corrupts the product organisation — teams ship expansion features nobody wants to lift NRR, or cut support to lift margin — and that the durable move is to build the machine and let metrics follow. Their evidence: the same repricing cycle produced a cohort of companies with beautiful dashboards and hollowed-out products. Both are right about the failure they name; neither has a general rule for when the other's failure dominates.

On valuation versus dilution. Growth-oriented practitioners argue for the highest clean price available, on the logic that dilution is permanent and momentum is self-fulfilling. Efficiency-oriented practitioners argue for raising less at a defensible price, because a high mark is a covenant and down rounds destroy more value than dilution does. The evidence is genuinely mixed: the 2021 cohort supports the second view; the winners of the 2010s often support the first.

On AI defensibility. Some serious investors believe application-layer AI companies are structurally advantaged — proprietary workflow data and switching costs compound. Others believe most of them are thin wrappers whose margin and differentiation are rented from a foundation model and will be reclaimed. Nobody has enough renewal data yet to settle it, and both sides are deploying capital on their conviction. This is the live frontier of the topic, and a PM should expect the board question to be asked in a different form every six months.

Section ElevenDecisions, and Questions for Discussion

Priya raised £5.5m in July at a valuation 30% below what a growth-at-any-price story might have supported. She presented the 91% NRR on slide four rather than burying it, stated the multi-site sample size before the result, and committed publicly to the M15 proof. Two funds passed on the grounds of market ceiling — a portfolio-construction objection she had predicted. The fund that led had a smaller vehicle and different mathematics. Her reasoning: the lower price bought a milestone she could actually hit, and the disclosure bought credibility she would need in eighteen months.

Marcus split the difference in a way his lead investor initially disliked. He allocated $2.6m to margin work and $1.4m to a single additional carrier chosen specifically because its logo de-risked the concentration problem, and he renegotiated one of the two Q4 renewals into a three-year agreement six months early, accepting an 11% price concession to move the renewal outside the raise window. His reasoning: margin is the proof that takes longest to manufacture and is most damaging when discovered by someone else; logos can be bought faster; and concentration can be defused by contract structure rather than by sales.

1. Priya accepted a 30% valuation discount to make her milestone achievable. Under what conditions is that trade wrong — and how would she know before the next round rather than after?

2. Marcus spent $2.6m on gross margin, which produces no new revenue. How should a board evaluate spending that improves the denominator of a metric rather than the numerator of the business?

3. Both protagonists chose to disclose a weakness early. Is early disclosure a reliably dominant strategy, or does it depend on the thickness of the funding market at that moment?

Section TwelveGoing Deeper

  • Cash flow, burn and runway — the constraint that makes fundraising necessary; every argument above collapses to its arithmetic.
  • Board and investor communication — how the proofs assembled here are sequenced, disclosed and defended between rounds.
  • Strategy when you are the founder — what changes when you are choosing the milestone rather than serving it.
  • Unit economics — the model you should build rather than read about; Latchkey's whole case is a unit-economics argument.
  • CAC, LTV and payback — the acquisition half of the Series A proof, and where payback beats LTV as a diagnostic.
  • SaaS metrics: ARR, MRR, churn, NRR — the vocabulary boards use; NRR is where product architecture meets valuation.
  • Gross margin and cost to serve — the number that killed the cautionary comparator and rebuilt it.
  • Contribution margin — the right lens when acquisition spend is variable, as in marketplaces and consumer.
  • Reading a P&L — the statement your decomposition arguments must ultimately reconcile to.
Teaching note: this explainer is written for classroom use. Latchkey and Verity Loop are composites; the numbers are internally consistent and chosen to reward decomposition rather than recall.
